en: The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* is the secondary axis of the Mahāyāna. It erects the supreme banner of the True Dharma, refutes heterodox schools in its own time,
distinguishes between the false and the true in later ages, turns the Wheel of Brahmā during the Semblance Age, and continues the lineage for a thousand years.
This is the lingering influence of that [past].
It has caused the wheel of the sheep and the deer to cease its chariot, while the wheel of the *dharmacakra* (the supreme wheel) is opened anew.
Regarding its emergence: it occurred more than one thousand one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
However, because the time since the Sage departed has been so long and the True Dharma has declined,
the various heterodoxies have cast their shadows across the path while narrow attachments intersect at every turn;
consequently, the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) has remained hidden and its transmission obstructed.
At that time, there appeared in the world four bodhisattvas known as Asaṅga,
which in this language means "Unattached."
They are also called "unimpeded.
Such individuals inwardly dwell in the realm of the Dharma-nature,
while outwardly responding to the various capacities of sentient beings to assist in bringing forth the rain of the Dharma.
Gathering the sublime marks of the two kings and recording the Dharma-seal of the three natures,
he desires that sentient beings and their mental states may awaken to the true reality of non-abiding within Vijñapti-mātra.
Consequently, he composed this treatise in reliance upon the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
Now, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu— this is translated as Tianqin (Heavenly Relative)— is as follows:
That person’s wisdom that accords with reality was internally integrated,
and their understanding that accords with phenomena blossomed brilliantly.

[He] sighed with admiration that the words and meanings of this fundamental treatise were profound and abstruse, fearing that sentient beings of future generations might harbor delusions and fail to awaken.
Thereupon, he immediately began to investigate and determine the essential points, composing a commentary to explain the original text.
Thus, he refuted the Two Vehicles to return to the One Vehicle;
having crushed divergent views, all were brought together into a single mind.
Thus, the Way of Consciousness-Only was once again made accessible,
and the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature was here once more revealed.
Second, the delimitation of the categories included within the Tripiṭaka is explained.
However, while the principles revealed are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
we shall now discuss them according to their essentials.
Since there are three objects to be explained (*vācya*), the teachings (*deśanā*) are likewise threefold.
Because there are two types of intended audiences, the teachings are likewise twofold.
As for the threefold classification,
the first is called Sūtra.
This term "cord" (yàn) is also called "sutra" (jīng).
This is because a cord can string together flowers, while a sutra can hold together the warp; their functional meanings are thus analogous.
However, because this region values the title of the scripture itself rather than the honorific designation for the translator,
translators here follow what is valued; thus,
they omit the translator's name while retaining it in the title of the scripture.

Just as the teachings of the Sage can penetrate the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) so that they are not lost or corrupted, and cause the Dharma to endure for a long time— resembling the warp and woof of a thread—
it is named after this analogy.
This refers to the teaching that defines meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
*Vinaya* means "extinguishing.
This is because the evils of body, speech, and mind burn the practitioner; the meaning is the same as fire blazing.
Because the precepts can extinguish [defilements], they are called "extinction" (*nirodha*);

this name is derived from their functional capacity. The teaching that explains them is also called "extinction," as it refers to the teaching that elucidates the practice of the precepts. Third is the Abhidharma.
This is called the "Incomparable Dharma" (Abhidharma) and is also called the "Dharma Corresponding to Wisdom" (Abhidharma).
To destroy the afflictions and discern the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*),
non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-prajñā*) is the most preeminent.
Because there is no other dharma that can be compared to this, it is called the "Incomparable Dharma" (anupamadharmā).
This name is derived from its lack of counterpart.
Since the teaching follows that which is expressed, it is also called the "Incomparable Dharma."
This refers to the teaching that elucidates wisdom.
If it is called "Abhidharma," then "abhi" signifies the counteracting wisdom.
Dharma is the phenomenon that serves as the object of cognition;
thus, its name is established based on its objective function.
These latter two Piṭakas both derive their names from what they expound.
Question:
If that is so, why does the subsequent commentary state:
The Sūtras are established separately to explain the three types of training;
the Vinaya is established to accomplish the training based on ethical discipline and the training based on the mind.
This is verified by these texts.
The Sūtras should be understood as elucidating the three types of conduct, while the Vinaya elucidates the two types of conduct. Answer:
There are two meanings.
The gate of mutual accomplishment through a single characteristic:
the practices of the three trainings mutually assist and accomplish one another,
and the teachings that express them likewise possess both auxiliary and primary aspects.
This text simultaneously explains and clarifies the auxiliary [factors], which is why it is said that "the three are taught.
The intent of establishing these two tenets is to establish the clarification of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because it distinguishes between the fundamental and the derivative, the Abhidharma does not discuss the principle of the [auxiliary factors].
In reality, it applies to both.
Second, regarding the gate of defining their essential natures:
although the sūtras speak of precepts and wisdom, [the former]...
This belongs specifically to the Vinaya-abhidharma;
although mental discipline is discussed within the Abhidharma,
its specific classification likewise pertains to the other two Piṭakas.
The *Vibhāṣā* also provides these two explanations.
This treatise is subsumed within the Abhidharma Piṭaka. Regarding the two types of intended recipients, there is a distinction between those with sharp and dull faculties.
Regarding the Dharma, there are differences of depth and shallowness.
For those of dull faculties, the Śrāvakas, the Three Piṭakas are established based on the nature of conceptual construction (parikalpita-svabhāva),
in order to accomplish the practices of the Śrāvaka path.
It is classified as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka,
based on the eleven types of matter,
fourteen dissociated factors, and forty-seven mental states and mental concomitants established by the Śrāvakas.
Together with the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*),
these seventy-five dharmas are all *vastu-dharmas* (substantial phenomena) and therefore belong to the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

For Bodhisattvas of sharp faculties, [the teachings] are established as the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) by comprehensively encompassing the natures of discrimination, dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Because it is for the purpose of accomplishing the practices and dharmas of a bodhisattva,
it is classified as the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Question:
The Sūtra states:
"For the sake of the various pratyekabuddhas, he taught the method of contemplating dependent origination.
Thus, the pratyekabuddhas also possess the teaching.
Why is it that the Piṭakas are not established?
Answer:
According to the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*.
The teachings of the three vehicles establish three piṭakas.
Now, according to this treatise and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*,
the reason why a Piṭaka of Pratyekabuddhas is not established is as follows:
Regarding those who practice the contemplation of causes and conditions based on a semblance of the Buddha,
this refers to attaining awakening through what resembles hearing the voice of another;
they are categorized as being identical to the śrāvakas and are thus judged to be included within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.

This refers exclusively to those of superior capacity who have attained the higher path; appearing during a time when the Buddha-dharma does not exist and no teachings can be heard, they ought to realize the causes and conditions for themselves through the power of contemplation and cultivation, thereby attaining the fruit of the Way.
Because there is practice, the vehicles (yāna) can be established;
because there is no teaching to be heard [in that regard], the collections (piṭaka) are not established.
Within the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, there are two.
First is the teaching door of establishing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This refers to those who, while understanding that there is no self (*ātman*) within the harmonious combination of the aggregates (*skandha*),
nevertheless conceive of fixed natures in the distinct phenomena such as the aggregates themselves.
As it is said: they cling to form as having the intrinsic nature of form, and to the mind as having the intrinsic nature of mind;
they hold that all phenomena of the three times possess a fixed nature.
This is because they have not yet attained the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Second is the teaching that refutes [the existence of] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The faculties of these individuals are somewhat sharp;
they also understand the non-existence of a self-soul (*ātman*).
Knowing that the aggregates and other distinct phenomena exist because they arise from a collection of conditions, and thus lack an original intrinsic nature—
this is precisely the analytical realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Although the contemplative understanding of these two individuals differs in its depth, [they both realize this].

Because they likewise seem to awaken to the minor fruits upon hearing the voices of others, they are collectively categorized as the Śrāvaka Piṭaka in relation to their intended audience. Within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, there are two parts:
first is the Piṭaka of Revealed Teaching.
This refers to the elimination of all phenomena within the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
As the Sūtra says: "Form is empty, up to and including Nirvāṇa, which is ultimately empty in its essence.
This is the signless Mahāyāna, also known as the teaching of the revealed gate.

Second, regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it explains the reality of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*), such as the reality of *tathatā* (suchness) and the stainless dharmas.
This is precisely the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) of the Mahāyāna, the vehicle of the natural state (*prakṛtistha-yāna*), also known as the gateway of the secret teaching.
Although the meanings expressed by these two differ in their relative depth,
they are both categorized collectively as the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, because they are intended for bodhisattvas of sharp faculties who advance toward great practice and awaken to the great fruit.
This treatise encompasses both of the two teachings.
If it speaks of the three natures, emptiness, and so forth, it is the explicit teaching;
if it speaks of the initial characteristics and so forth, it is subsumed under the secret teaching.
Regarding the third point, the fundamental tenets elucidated by the Mingjiao (Clarifying the Teaching) school:
according to the meaning of the subsequent text, there are two types of fundamental tenets.
The first is categorized according to the Two Truths.
Second, regarding the Buddha-nature: as for the two truths, if one discusses the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) is the primary tenet to be elucidated.
If one speaks of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the two-fold selflessness is the primary tenet to be elucidated.
Therefore, the subsequent commentary states:
"All phenomena take consciousness as their characteristic and take true thusness as their essence."
It further states:
"To know that objects have no existence is to penetrate the ultimate (paramārtha-satya);
to know that there is only consciousness is to penetrate the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya). Second, regarding their nature:
Discussing the intention behind the sages' establishment of the teachings:
it is precisely because they wish to manifest the principle, accomplish practice, and through the accomplishment of practice, attain the fruit.
The first two superior characteristics are the Buddha-nature abiding in its own nature (*prakṛtistha-gotra*).
Among these, regarding the first, the preeminent characteristic:
if one discusses the function of the mind, it is the causal condition as it truly is;
if one relies on its actual reality, it is the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the mind.
Therefore, the subsequent explanation states:
"This very dhātu of ālayavijñāna has understanding as its nature;
this dhātu possesses five meanings, and so forth."
It is also called the non-empty tathāgatagarbha.

The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* also clarifies that taking the ālayavijñāna as the object for the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is precisely the true suchness of mind (*cittatathatā*). Why is this so?
This is the contemplation of defilement and its basis.
This clarifies that the functional capacity of the mind serves as the basis for the defiled phenomena of the twelve links of dependent origination;
it is precisely the suchness of causes and conditions.
Within the second supreme characteristic:
if one considers the characteristics themselves, the three natures are the results produced by prior causes and conditions.

If one relies on the reality [of things], the three natures fundamentally do not exist; thus, the absence of the three natures is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā) and "true suchness" (tathatā), and is also termed the "empty tathāgatagarbha."
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
"Because grasping does not exist, the three natures are established as being without nature.
This [emptiness] is subsumed within the two aspects of True Suchness: emptiness and non-emptiness.
Because the two realities are non-dual,
the first two superior characteristics are termed the "buddha-nature abiding in its own nature" (*svabhāva-vyavasthita-gotra*).
The six superior characteristics within that interval are termed the "buddha-nature brought forth" (*nirmocana-gotra*).
Because it manifests the principle of abiding in one's own nature by overcoming obstacles through the perfection of practice, it is called "induced.
The latter two superior characteristics are termed "attaining the fruit" Buddha-nature;

because one attains the stage of the fruit, the previously existing causes—namely the cause of abiding in one's own nature and the induced cause—are realized, and thus it is called "attaining the fruit."
The Sage established the teachings with the intent of accomplishing these three;
thus, the three kinds of Buddha-nature constitute the primary tenets to be expounded.
Therefore, the text below states:
If one wishes to explain the essence of the Buddha as well as its causes and effects, their number is exactly thus; therefore, they are taught in this sequence.
Thus, it should be known that the ten superior characteristics are the three kinds of Buddha-nature.
Regarding the treatise on the nature of the teaching that expresses [the truth],
there are two reasons why the school that adheres to the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) [asserts] that sound is a material phenomenon (rūpadharma) as its essence. Thus, that treatise states:
Because the Buddha’s words are intended to convey meaning,
[the Sautrāntika school] maintains that they take as their essence non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) such as names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*).
The Śūnyatāvāda school (Dharmalakṣaṇa) refutes this, asserting that from the second moment onward, they take as their essence a continuity that resembles sound.
This is subsumed under the *dharmāyatana* and is known by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
because the Mahāyāna school holds that its essence consists of the cognition of form (*rūpavijñapti*) which resembles the nature of sound.
It refers to the names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) expressed by sound.
The Title of the Fourth Commentary on the Śāstra: Regarding what is called "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*), there are generally four types of inclusion when discussed broadly.
The first is the inclusion of the text by means of the text.
For example, if one takes the four characters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* as the basis, they encompass the entirety of that body of scriptural teachings;
thus, the text below states:
"Furthermore, because the sections mutually encompass their respective categories, they are called 'Pitakas' (collections)."
Second, the inclusion of meanings by means of meaning.
This is because, taking the characteristic of the basis as fundamental, all meanings are fully subsumed.
As the text below states:
This basis is said to be "comprised" because it is the storehouse (pitaka) that serves as the support for the nine meanings, such as "that which is to be known.
Third, the text is comprised by its meaning,
because all literary expressions are established in dependence upon meaning.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise clarifies that it is called "retention" (*dhāraṇī*) because, by realizing the principle of *tathatā*, one is able to encompass both the words and their meaning.
Fourth, the meaning is encompassed by the words.
This refers precisely to the treatise *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Although the text of the treatise is concise,
it comprehensively subsumes the meanings expounded by all the various Mahāyāna schools.
This constitutes a collection of ten kinds of superior characteristics.
Because this passage below summarizes the meaning through its phrasing, it is called a "collection" (*saṃgraha*). Regarding the term "great," there are three types:
first, greatness of essence (*tattva-mahattva*).
This is because, in the present moment, the two kinds of *tathatā*— emptiness and non-emptiness— are equal and subject to neither increase nor decrease.
Second is the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahattva*), which refers to the fact that upon the essence of *tathatā* there are the distinctions of countless, untainted, inherent merits.
Regarding the greatness of name and appearance: because each and every virtue is universally pervasive throughout the dharma-realm and is eternal, it is called "Great.
Third is the greatness of function.
That is to say, this very Suchness (tathatā) possesses, in the state of causality, functions such as sustaining defilement and purity and inwardly perfuming;
upon reaching the state of fruition, it possesses functions such as manifesting the two bodies—the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and the enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya)—and the nirvana without abode.
Because each and every function is pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm and is eternal,
it is called "Great.
Although from the perspective of deluded views there may be decline or flourishing, [the essence remains unchanged].
"By means of constancy. There are three kinds of vehicles (*yāna*):
first, the vehicle of principle (*li-yāna*), which is the naturally abiding Buddha-nature (*prakṛtistha-gotra*) characterized by the two supreme aspects mentioned previously.
Second is the vehicle of practice (*pratipatti-yāna*),
which refers to the six superior characteristics that draw forth the Buddha-nature.
Third is the vehicle of fruition (*phala-yāna*).
This refers to the latter two superior characteristics, namely the Buddha-nature as the fruit of supreme virtue;
thus, the sub-commentary below clarifies that the "Vehicle" has three meanings.
First, the single nature;
second, conformity;
third, virtue.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time rely upon this vehicle;
because this Dharma distinguishes the stage of the Tathāgata, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*). There are four types of treatises (*śāstra*):
first, the difficult treatise (*durlabha-śāstra*).
The first is the class of treatises on reasoning, such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*. The second is the class of treatises that collect and synthesize meaning,
such as the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Third, treatises that explain the essential tenets (*śāstra-vyākhyāna*),
such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa*.
Fourth, treatises that explain the literal text (*grantha-vyākhyāna*).
As in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, and other such works,
these four types are collectively termed "treatises" (*śāstra*).

They are called treatises because they employ the method of debate— whereby a host and a guest engage in a process of mutual inquiry, refutation, and the investigation of principles through question and answer.
As for the basis, this ālayavijñāna is the support for all phenomena.
Among all bases, this consciousness is supreme; therefore, it is called the "supreme characteristic."
Because these characteristics contain four categories, they are called "middle.
Regarding the term "assembly" (*gaṇa*), it refers to the basis of sustenance;
because this term appears first, it is called the "first."
There are three ways in which the Three Jewels are not distinct. First is their common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):
this refers to the principle of Buddha-nature being divided into three.
Specifically, the meaning of the nature-principle’s awakening and illumination is the Buddha.
The meaning of "normative rules" (niyama) is the Dharma;
the meaning of "monastic community" (saṃgha) is the harmonious proclamation of that same nature.

Although there are these three meanings, their essence is one and not different; therefore, they are called the "common characteristics" (sādharmya). Second, as for the Three Jewels with distinct characteristics (vaidharmya):
The first is named Jewel Buddha (Ratnabuddha).
His Dharma-body takes the true and eternal five aggregates as its essence;
his Reward-body takes the five aggregates accomplished through cultivation as its essence.
The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) takes the five aggregates as its substance through the function of transformation.
Principles, teachings, practices, and fruits are termed the Dharma;
Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and the Saṃgha constitute the Saṃgha. These are the three Treasures of Sustenance.
They take images of the Buddha and the like as the Buddha;
texts written on paper, silk, and other materials as the Dharma;
and Ānanda, Kāśyapa, and others, as well as ordinary bhikṣus, as the embodiment of the Saṃgha.
If the images of the Sangha, such as those of Ānanda and Kāśyapa, as well as the Buddha and the Dharma, all take the four sense-objects (*catur-viṣaya*) as their substance;
and if one takes the ordinary Sangha (*pṛthagjana-saṃgha*) as having the five out-flowing aggregates (*sāsrava-pañca-skandha*) as its substance.
The meaning of the Tripiṭaka is analyzed through two gates:
*Sūtra* is here translated as "sutra" (cord), because it is able to connect and maintain the characteristics of all phenomena; *Vinaya* is named "extinction."
It is not because the karma of body and speech has been extinguished;
rather, these two receive their names based on their functional significance. Regarding the Abhidharma, there are two [interpretations]:
first, it is said to mean "incomparable dharma" (anuttara-dharma).
The name is derived from its formal characteristics and ultimate meaning.
Second is the "Dharma of Counteraction," because the objects of observation and the dharmas attained therein are that which is countered.
Wisdom is that which acts as the counteragent;
this is a general designation applied to the union of object and mind.
As for "pitaka" (basket), the name is established according to its meaning. Second, to clarify the essence:
The Tripiṭaka is identical in taking sound, form, and consciousness as its substance.
The two Piṭakas are analyzed according to two gates of meaning:
first, the name; second, the meaning.
First are the bodhisattvas,
and second are the śrāvakas.
The teaching for those of superior faculties who practice the conduct of the two benefits is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Those of inferior faculties who practice for their own benefit and are taught the path of self-benefit are called Śrāvakas. Second, the clarification of the essence:
although two distinct types are established based on the individuals, in terms of their essence, they are the same as the aforementioned three Piṭakas.
There are nine causes for establishing the Piṭakas.
Regarding the meaning of the term "cause" (*hetu*), there are three pairs of three. First, they are divided into three according to the obstacles:
first, the obstacle of the division of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This is solely the method of cultivation.
Second is the obstacle of karma,
namely the three unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
It arises from the two extremes of suffering and pleasure.
Third is the obstacle of self-view and grasping (satkāyadṛṣṭi-parāmarśa),
which takes various views as its primary head and consists of the ten afflictions (daśa-kleśa) that delude one regarding the principle.
Regarding the two types of essence:
the first and last two types have the mind as their nature, while the middle one has all three types of action as its essence. Second, regarding the three [types]:
The Sūtras are said to fully explain the three trainings because they comprehensively explain both the fundamental and the derivative;
furthermore, the Sūtra is the teaching.
The three trainings and the three gates are all produced based on the teaching; therefore, this statement is made.
The Vinaya accomplishes two [trainings], because concentration is produced based on ethical discipline; therefore, this statement is made.
Abhidharma is exclusively wisdom (*prajñā*);
because this [wisdom] is yet to be fully known, it is simply called "wisdom. Third, the three are the meaning of the Dharma (*dharmārtha*).
Proclaiming the meaning of the Dharma—the causes and conditions—is the Sūtra.
Because this treasury proclaims the linguistic expressions,
it accomplishes the Dharma, its meaning, and the Vinaya;
for since there is no doubt regarding what is upheld or transgressed, it establishes the Dharma and its meaning as cause and effect.
The superior wisdom regarding the meaning of the Dharma arises from the Abhidharma;
because this Piṭaka generates superior knowledge, one is able to comprehend the meaning of the Dharma.
The meaning of "absence of regret" is analyzed through ten factors and two gates.
First, maintaining the precepts;
second, freedom from remorse;
third, peace of mind.
Fourth, attaining joy;
fifth, inquiring about serenity;
sixth, delight.
Seventh, meditative concentration;
eighth, seeing things as they truly are;
ninth, wearying detachment.
Regarding the two natures of the ten liberations:
among these, within the first six,
the first one has the observance of precepts as its cause.
The latter five are the fruits of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
They are all subsumed under the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) and are collectively causes for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The seventh is the fruit of concentration,
which is the cause of wisdom.
The eighth is the fruit of wisdom.
The ninth is the function of wisdom.
The tenth is the fruit of the inquiry into the three trainings.
If one establishes their essential nature according to the three types of action:
The first [of these] pervades all three types of action;
the middle eight have mind alone as their essence;
and the last one has the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) as its essence.
Regarding the three trainings:
the first six are ethical discipline;
the middle one is meditative concentration.
The next two [factors] are wisdom (*prajñā*).
The last one is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fruit obtained from the preceding three.
The Tripiṭaka generally employs five meanings for the threefold classification system.
First, the name;
second, the essence;
third, the abiding ground. Regarding the first, the name:
These are: perfuming (vāsanā), awakening (prativedha), tranquility (śama), penetration (pratisaṃvit), and liberation (vimukti).
Regarding "perfuming": through the continuous practice of hearing and reflection, it perfumes consciousness so as to form seeds;
this name is derived from a metaphor.
The "Awakened" (Buddha) is so named because, through the power of cultivated wisdom, they are able to perceive the truth; thus, they are called "Awakened.
The "Quiescent" (Śānta) is so named because they have distanced themselves from the grasping of subject and object; thus, they are called "Quiescent.
As for "Pervasive" (Vyāpin), if there were grasping at subject and object, one would not be pervasive.
Because there is neither subject nor object and because it is equanimous, it is pervasive.
As for liberation: if one does not penetrate the true principle, one cannot be liberated;
it is by attaining realization of the principle that one achieves liberation.
The names of the latter four are established based on the excellence of the predominant function of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Regarding their essential natures (*svabhāva*): the first [the *śrutamayī*] has the nature of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*), while the middle three have cultivated wisdom as their essence.
The latter type takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its essence. Regarding the three stages:
if one considers them generally, each individual stage possesses these five meanings;
however, if they are distinguished specifically:
Perfuming occurs prior to the first stage;
awakening occurs at the first stage;
and tranquility occurs from the second stage through the seventh stage.
The general [application] extends from the eighth stage to the tenth stage, while liberation resides in the Buddha-stage.

There are four distinct meanings. Regarding the *sūtra*, there is a twofold analysis of name and essence. As for the "name": [The text continues: ...the four meanings... the two gates of analysis... the name... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a technical commentary on Buddhist scholastic categories, specifically concerning the stages (*bhūmi*) of realization and the structural analysis of the *sūtra*.)
First, the basis (*āśraya*),
because it serves as the foundation for the teaching for those who dwell therein;
second, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
This refers to the three dharmas— such as the ultimate and the conventional, identity and difference, and self and other—
which are called "dharmas" because they constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
Regarding the four meanings:
they are called "meanings" (*artha*) because they signify functional utility. Regarding the two natures (*svabhāva*):
the nature is established based on the substance, taking the qualities of the supreme function—ranging from form (*rūpa*) up to subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)—as its essence.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) take the ultimate and conventional natures of all phenomena as their essence.
"Phenomena" (dharma) take the aggregates and so forth as their substance.
"Meaning" (artha) takes the teachings of the doctrine as its essence.
Because this dharma serves as the basis for generating the path that extinguishes transgressions against the precepts,
the meaning of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) is analyzed through two approaches:
first, the names of the aggregates.
The two entities: one is the general name "existence" (bhava) and the other is the specific name "five aggregates" (pañca-skandhāḥ).
Regarding the five aggregates:
"five" is a number.
"Skandha" means an accumulation (*caya*).
It is named according to its numerical meaning, as understood through the skandhas.
The specific [skandhas] are form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The obstruction of form is resolved through matter;
the experience of sensation is clarified through feeling;
and the grasping of characteristics constitutes perception.
"Forming" (*saṃskāra*) has the meaning of "arising as activity.
"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is "discernment" (*vijñapti*).
These are designated by their common function and result. They are two entities.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) has the consciousness of form as its intrinsic nature.
The middle three aggregates have mental factors (caitasika-dharma) as their intrinsic nature according to their respective functions.
Furthermore, among the formations (saṃskāra), it is not possible for them to be the bodily, vocal, or mental karmas.
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) takes the sixth, seventh, and eighth [consciousnesses] as its substance;
it is analyzed by way of two doors within the eighteen elements (dhātu).
First, by name:
Regarding the two substances:
as for "names," one divides the preceding form (*rūpa*) into the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*);
one takes the preceding three aggregates (*skandha*) to constitute the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*).
Using the aforementioned aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the elements (*dhātu*), there are the six consciousness-elements.
The six objects (*viṣaya*) refer to form, sound, odor, taste, and so forth.
The six faculties (*indriya*) refer to the eye-element, ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, body-element, and mind-element.
The six consciousnesses share the same name as their bases (indriya) and their substance (svabhāva).
Since they are identical to the aggregates (skandha), no further differentiation is required.

Regarding the twelve bases (āyatana): their names and substances refer to the six objects (viṣaya). These ten dharmas are the bases for consciousness; thus, they are called "bases" (āyatana) because they are the entry points [for consciousness].
The name is derived from its meaning. As for its essence (*tī*), it is not different from the aggregates (*skandha*);
it is merely designated as an "entrance" (*āyatana*) based on its meaning.
The meaning of the Four Noble Truths is analyzed through two gates:
first, their names;
second, their essence. They are collectively termed "truths" (*satya*) because they are real.
Therefore, they are called "truths" (*satya*). As for their names, they are suffering (*duḥkha*), origination (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*).
"Suffering" (duḥkha) has the meaning of oppression;
"origination" (samudaya) has the meaning of summoning and inducing.
These two names are received according to their respective meanings of fault.
"Nirvāṇa" (nirodha) is so called because it can extinguish the fires of the three poisons;
"the Path" (mārga) has the meaning of being able to produce [realization].
These two are named according to their functional activity. As for their essence, there are two types.
First, regarding characteristics:
the essential characteristic is established by taking the principles of suffering, impermanence, and so forth as the nature of suffering.
The principle of causality and so forth constitutes the origin;
the principles of the path and so forth constitute the path;
and the principle of perfect cessation constitutes cessation.
This is explained from the perspective of characteristics;
secondly, from the perspective of reality.
In the Mahāyāna, the single-flavored *tathatā* (suchness) itself is the reality of suffering.
Even unto the reality of the essence of the Path,
as the Sūtra says:
"That which exists as real is the unconditioned Four Noble Truths."
Next, the definition is clarified through a twofold classification:
first, the name;
second, the essence. Regarding the name:
This refers to the stages of the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
"Dhyāna" is termed "cultivation through reflection" (bhāvanā) and is also called a "grove of merit.
It has two aspects.
The fourth dhyāna has eighteen factors;
these constitute its essential nature.
There are eighteen dhyāna-factors.
The first dhyāna has five factors:
vitarka and vicāra serve as the antidote,
while prīti and sukha constitute the benefit.
One-pointedness of mind is the essence of concentration; the second dhyāna has four factors:
internal clarity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
Internal clarity is the antidote.
The middle two [factors] are benefits;
the final one mind is the essence of concentration.
The third dhyāna has five factors.
One practices equanimity, pure mindfulness, and settled discernment.
Equanimity, mindfulness, and discernment are the remedies;
pleasure is the benefit.
One-pointedness of mind is the essence;
one delights in one-pointedness of mind.
The four dhyānas each have four factors.
Equanimity and mindfulness, neither suffering nor pleasure, and one-pointedness—this equanimity and mindfulness is the remedy.
Neither suffering nor pleasure is the benefit.
One-pointedness is the essence of concentration. These are the two essences.
It consists of nine factors, namely:
vitarka, vicāra, vedanā, praśrabdhi, samādhi, upekṣā, smṛti, prajñā, and chanda.
The factor of vedanā is divided into four types.
The factors of serenity (praśrabdhi) are divided into two;
that is, within the first two dhyānas, the blissful application (sukha-prahāṇa), equanimity (upekṣā), and mindfulness (smṛti) are each divided into two.
The factors of concentration (samādhi) are divided into four.
The remaining four are not divided.
Regarding the meaning, name, and substance of the four formless [attainments]: as for the names, they are first, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The second is the sphere of infinite consciousness,
and the third is the sphere of nothingness;
both are named according to the characteristics of their preparatory practices.
Fourth, because one practices by forming an understanding of emptiness, consciousness, and so forth within the context of skillful means,
it is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This name is established based on the sense of transcending the characteristics and forms [of perception].
To call it "non-conceptual" based on its external form is an error,
for in reality there still exists subtle conceptualization. As for its essence,
it takes the four aggregates and the mind as its substance.
As for why the factors are not established separately for the upper and lower realms:
it is because these [lower realms] constitute the path of suffering,
whereas the factors are established for the path of happiness.
The path of suffering does not establish its constituent factors (*aṅga*);
the same applies to the limits of the four dhyānas.
Regarding the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), their meaning is their name and their essence. As for the name:
Earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, space, and consciousness—
these ten factors are each pervasive throughout all things without interval, and are thus called "pervasive" (vibhūta).
They are called "entrances" (āyatana) because they serve as the conditions for consciousness.
The general names are derived from their number and meaning;
the specific names are derived from their objects. Regarding their two natures:
in the Hīnayāna, the first eight have the roots of goodness associated with non-contention as their nature.
The "retinue" consists of the four aggregates or five aggregates.
Emptiness and consciousness take the four aggregates as their substance.
In the Mahāyāna, both likewise take the wisdom of "consciousness-only without external objects" as their substance.
Alternatively, it may take mental discourse as its essence, which is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The three types of wisdom (*jñāna*) are distinguished as being merely the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*).
Regarding the two kinds of distinctions for the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), they are termed "name" and "essence. As for "name":
One who is "without contention" protects sentient beings through five causes so that they do not give rise to afflictions and do not contend with others;
thus, the name is established based on the absence of fault. Second is the essence.
It clarifies that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas protect sentient beings through the wisdom of things as they are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and great compassion;
this wisdom of things as they are constitutes their essence.
The Hīnayāna, however, takes conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) as its essence.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, [the term] is obtained only by the noble ones (*ārya*).
It takes as its essence the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that functions through names.

Regarding the *Abhidharma*, there are four meanings and two names; its essence consists of: first, opposition (*pratipakṣa*); second, enumeration (*saṃkhyā*); third, subduing (*abhibhava*); and fourth, comprehension (*parijñā*).
Regarding "the counterpart":
saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are that which is countered,
while wisdom is that which counters.
Names are established based on the meaning of their characteristics and forms.
As for "number," it refers to clearly explaining a single dharma by manifesting its layers of profundity.
"Subduing" (vaśī-bhūta) means that which is able to subdue all [opposing] doctrines;
"understanding" (vid) means...
Because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the teachings of the first two baskets are clearly visible through these instructions, they are called "explanation" (*vyākhyā*).
These three [baskets] are established by name according to their predominant functional efficacy (*vṛtti*). As for their essence (*svabhāva*):
It takes only the scriptural teachings as its essence.
Although the four meanings are clarified in terms of what is expressed,
the statement that the teachings possess this superior function is equivalent to explaining the essence of the teaching.
If one takes the functional essence produced from that [grasping], it has the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) as its essence.
The nine kinds of skillful means are set forth in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
One subdues and refutes by means of the five-membered syllogism—
namely, the five members beginning with the thesis—
and challenges that thesis by means of the four types of skillful means.
Regarding that, two skillful means are established:
first, whether the five factors are complete;
second, even if the five factors are complete, whether one is free from the three faults.
This constitutes the fallacies of contradiction, unreality, and uncertainty;
if all three faults are present, there is no need for refutation, as it collapses of its own accord.
Second, examining the opponent's objection also requires two skillful means.
First, examine whether the fivefold division is complete;
second, one must recognize the opponent's intention to retreat.
However, that opponent merely feels ashamed to accept defeat.
Without personally accepting defeat, he said,
"Let us cease for now and await further discussion later," thereby causing his opponent to submit immediately upon these words.
If one explains it without understanding that speech, one is simply ignorant;
therefore, one must understand that intention regarding their regression.
There are two meanings of the eight expedient means.
First, the name;
second, the essence. Regarding the name:
the five-membered syllogism consists of five parts.
First, the formal proposition;
second, the citation of scriptural evidence;
third, the analogy.
The four analogies,
the five fetters,
and the three skillful means.
Contradiction, unreality,
and uncertainty are refuted by means of the five members;
those [faults] are countered and destroyed by means of the three skillful methods.
It is established by subduing those [opposing views] through three skillful means. As for its essence (*tattva*):
although it is newly introduced according to the teaching, it takes the two types of wisdom—listening (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*)—as its essence.
If one proceeds according to the teaching itself, it takes consciousness (*vijñāna*) and sound (*śabda*) as its nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the names and natures of the two categories of five articles:
as for the first name, *pārājika*, this is translated as "extremely grave.
It is named according to its most serious transgression.
2. Saṃghāvaśeṣa—this is translated as "Saṃgha-remnant.
It refers to the impairment of monastic conduct such that it is incomplete; it is named according to what has been impaired and the transgression incurred.
3. Pāyattika—this is translated as "Falling."
They are named after their result, for by committing them one will inevitably fall into the evil realms; thus they are called *pātideśanīya*, which here means "to be confessed to another.
They are also named according to their remedial expedient.
The fifth is named *śaikṣā dharmāḥ*, which is translated here as "matters to be learned.
This name is established based on the capacity to prevent [unwholesome] conduct.
As for the general term "section" (*varga*): [it refers to a thematic grouping].
Those offenses that are equal in category are established in one place and designated as a "chapter" (varga);
this name is derived from their meaning. Second, regarding their substance:
they all have the performance of non-informative action (avijñapti) through body, speech, and mind as their substance.
If bodily and vocal actions are distinct, they have non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) as their essence;
mental action has volition (*cetanā*) as its essence. Regarding the seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*), one adds the group of misconduct (*kaukṛtya*) and the group of wrong speech (*durbhāṣita*).
Adding the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense),
which is here translated as "great obstacle to the Path," it receives its name because it involves misconduct and improper speech.
That which is performed by the body is called "evil action" (duṣkṛta), and that which is spoken by the mouth is called "evil speech" (durukta).
It is called a "great obstacle to the Path" because if one commits these, it will necessarily obstruct the Noble Path; hence, it is named a "great obstacle to the Path."
The name is derived from its transgression; its essential nature is the same as that of the five categories [of offenses], taking the actions of body, speech, and mind as its substance.
Its name is established based on the meaning of the four causes of origination.
First, ignorance:
by virtue of the wisdom that understands one's own ignorance,
there is no other established name for it.
Second is heedlessness (*pramāda*).
It is called "heedlessness" because it refers to the mental state of being negligent;
this is a designation based on its transgression.
Third, the intense proliferation of afflictions,
whereby, due to excessive lack of awareness, one gives rise to defilement, violates the precepts,
and deviates from the Path. Fourth, arrogance.
Because one holds the precepts lightly in mind and fails to give rise to reverence, one violates the Buddha’s precepts;
this name is established based on the transgression. Second, as for its essential nature:
ignorance is the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of nescience (*avidyā*).
Heedlessness is the underlying tendency of greed;
one becomes heedless because of greed.
The "blazing afflictions" refer to all afflictions, including both the two delusions of greed and hatred, as well as the envelopments and secondary defilements.
Contempt is exclusively the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*).
If one extracts its essential nature from among the three aggregates, it consists solely of the mind.
It is one of the eight types of instruments for creating karma.
One name, two entities. Regarding "name":
among the three types of karma, there are cases where [the result] arises from one [karma] and not from two;
and there are cases where it arises from two [karmas] and not from one.
To possess the three karmas is to possess one;
it is not by means of the three karmas that one possesses one.
It is by means of one that there are three.
First, by means of the mind and not by means of body or speech;
second, by means of the body and not by means of mind or speech;
third, by means of speech and not by means of mind or body.
Regarding "the existence of the three by means of two":
this refers to cases where [an action] arises from mind and body but not from speech;
or from body and speech but not from mind.
There are cases where one commits an offense through mind and speech, but not through body;
seven cases where one commits an offense through body, speech, and mind together;
and two meanings regarding cases where one commits an offense through neither mind, speech, nor body.

First, regarding the case where one employs a stratagem and subsequently regrets it, yet the offense of the person they dispatched is completed; because the offense is completed at the time of its fulfillment, the instructor incurs the guilt.
This does not depend on the three [factors].
Second, the same applies to using false speech to deceive a foreign woman.
At the initial moment, there is no offense because [the action] has not yet been committed;
later, at the time of the offense, the three karmas are likewise absent. As for their essence:
the two [karmas] of body and speech take form and consciousness as their essence.
The mind has mental consciousness as its nature.
Regarding the four names and two entities in the Vinaya:
as for the names, the first is "offense."
From the perspective of past experiences,
there are two conditions for origination;
these are the conditions for violating the precepts.
The name is established based on its meaning.
"Third, returning to purity" clarifies that the precepts return to being as pure as they were before.
Fourth is renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*), which clarifies the emergence from transgression.
These two [terms] are both named after their departure from faults. As for their essence (*tattva*):
The transgressions are distinguished according to the five categories and seven groups (*pañcāpatti-saptasaṃghāvaśeṣa*).
The origins (*nidāna*) are explained in either the four or the eight [precepts].
Purification and renunciation have as their essence the wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind through skillful means (*upāya*).
There are seven matters concerning renunciation (*naiṣkramya*): first, each [member] recites the *pāṭha* of the *mārga-śikṣāpada* according to its meaning, thereby deriving its name from that sense;
second, the acceptance of training and disciplinary penalties.
That is, names are established based on their meaning and application:
first, that which was originally prohibited is later permitted;
second, that which was further relinquished.
Five: the transformation of the basis of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
six: observation according to reality;
seven: the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
The names are derived from their respective meanings. Regarding the two substances (*tattva*):
each has as its nature the two karmas of body and speech initiated by the mind.
Alternatively, all three karmas may constitute their substance.
Second, the forfeiture and penalty for training (śikṣādaṇḍa) have the three karmas of body, speech, and mind as their intrinsic nature.
Third, that which was previously prohibited and subsequently permitted has form and consciousness as its substance.
Fourth, the further forfeiture is the same as the previous prohibition.
The five transformations of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) pertain exclusively to form (rūpa) and take form as their essence. The sixth,
the contemplation of reality as it is (yathābhūta-parīkṣā), takes the four seals of the Dharma— suffering, impermanence, non-self, and the tranquility of nirvāṇa— as its essence.
Suffering and impermanence are conditioned;
selflessness and the quiescent extinction of nirvāṇa are unconditioned.
These seven dharmas take the four noble truths as their essence.
In the Mahāyāna, the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) is taken as the essence of the Four Noble Truths;
what is termed "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) in the Hīnayāna is termed "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) in the Mahāyāna.
In this context, only those [teachings] that establish the four truths through formal composition are taken up.
Furthermore, the *Vinaya* has four meanings for its name and essence: first, the person;
this is named according to the numerical similarity [of the number of rules].
Second, the establishment of the precepts.
Having already explained the faults, the precept against non-celibacy was established;
having already explained the faults such as the censure of desire, [the precepts were established].
Third, the analysis:
having briefly established the regulation, it is now explained in detail.
That is to say, a bhikṣu wears a patched robe.
Fourth is the definitive judgment clarifying the characteristics of upholding and violating [the precepts] and so forth.
These three are all named according to their meaning.
Second, regarding the essence:
In general, these two [dharmas] take two dharmas as their essence.
It clarifies that the person has no essence and instead takes the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)—which are substantial dharmas—as its nature.
The latter three take form (*rūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their essence.
Because it has the nature of sound, there are ten superior characteristics regarding name and substance. Regarding "name":
first, the basis of what is to be known (*jñeyāśraya*).
The second should be known as such;
these two are named after their objects and their exhortative phrasing.
The third should be known as the entry.
It is named according to its object, its wisdom, and its exhortative phrasing.
The four [foundations of mindfulness] enter into cause and effect;
they are established by way of the wisdom to be accomplished and the practice that accomplishes it.
The fifth is the differentiation of the cultivation of cause and effect.
Cause and effect constitute practice;
cultivation constitutes the skillful means.
"Differentiation" refers to the stages.
These names are established based on the meaning of the stages of practice and the ability to cultivate skillful means.
As for the characteristics of the three trainings:
Precepts and so forth are the practice;
their substance is that which is relied upon.
Training is a function of the mind.
It is named according to its function in practice and the capacity of the mind.
The nine fruits of training (*śaikṣa-phala*) have the characteristic of quiescence (*śānti*); "training" (*śikṣā*) is the cause, and the "fruit" (*phala*) is the state (*avasthā*).
"Quiescence" (śama) is its meaning;
that is, the name is established based on the sense of the causal stage.
It consists of the distinctions of the ten knowledges.
Wisdom is the essence;
differentiation is its meaning.
It receives its name from this essence and its meaning.
The general name is "Excellence" (*viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*).
This name is established based on the meaning of being superior in form to the Lesser Vehicle and other [teachings]. Regarding the two bodies:
the first characteristic has the *ālayavijñāna* as its essence.
Second, by means of the three natures;
third, by means of the non-conceptual wisdom of consciousness-only;
fourth, by means of the practice of the six perfections as its essence.
Fifth, it takes the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as its nature.
Sixth, it takes the threefold aggregate of ethical conduct (*śīla-saṃvara*) as its essence.
Seventh, it takes the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) as its essence.
The eighth has the three wisdoms as its essence;
the ninth has non-abiding nirvana as its essence;
and the tenth has the three bodies as its essence.

The sublime teaching of the Sage possesses five kinds of excellence and has two names and essences: first, its correct exposition differs from the provisional teachings in that it is not a mere expedient;
second, it refutes the biased attachments of the Hīnayāna by directly confronting their incomplete understanding.
The third [characteristic] exists in the Mahāyāna but not in the Hīnayāna;
the fourth is the cause of great enlightenment (mahābodhi);
and the fifth brings sentient beings to the attainment of omniscience (sarvajñatā). As for its essence:
The first two take the Mahāyāna teachings as their essence;
that is, the latter three take the ten meanings as their essence.
Regarding the names of the essences according to the sequence of the three: first, there is the sequence of the object.
That which serves as the condition for the arising of consciousness is called the "object.
Second is the sequence of correct practice;
because the practice is not inverted, it is termed "correct practice."
The three fruits have a sequential order;
because they arise and subsequently fulfill their preceding causes, they are designated as "fruits.
These three are all names based on their functional meaning (*artha*). As for their two essential natures (*svabhāva*):
Its essence is identical to the preceding ten characteristics.
Since the first two characteristics are the objective realm,
they exist first and are subsequently empty.
The middle six are the practice,
which proceeds from inferior to superior;
the final two characteristics are the fruit.
This means that the dharma is mentioned first and the person second,
thereby clarifying their sequence.
The four principles are the names and essences [of the truths].
From the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*: First,
regarding the principle of cause and effect,
the initial characteristic is the universal cause.
The second characteristic is the common result;
the middle six are the specific causes;
and the final two are the specific results.
This does not contradict the general and specific causes and effects.
Second, the principle of mutual dependence refers to the mutual dependence of cause and effect, as well as the mutual dependence of the great and the small.
The third is the principle of establishment through proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*), which refers to the mutual establishment of the ten meanings by their characteristics. For example,
it is like the mutual establishment of non-arising and arising, or non-ceasing and ceasing, through their respective concordant and discordant characteristics.
Furthermore, the ten meanings herein are not inconsistent with the causes and fruits of bodhi;
therefore, the realization-wisdom (pramāṇa-jñāna) establishes these ten meanings as mere manifestations.
This is precisely the meaning of the five-membered syllogism (pañcāvayava-vākya), such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth.
The four dharmas are according to principle.

If all dharmas were such that their wisdom were identical to the suchness of those dharmas, yet each possessed a distinct substantial entity, then it would not accord with the principle of suchness; in that case, there would be three [distinct entities].
First, the suchness of selflessness;
second, the suchness of impermanence;
third, the suchness of tranquility. Regarding the two bodies:
The first three principles take the ten characteristics as their essence,
though they are divided into three based on their specific meanings;
the fourth has the principle of pervasion as its nature.
This is precisely the true suchness of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-tathatā*).
Regarding the names and entities of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
first is direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).
Whatever objects are known by ordinary beings or noble ones are not called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) when they belong to the past or future;
rather, the name is applied based on the meaning of the time in which the object is being cognized.
Second is scriptural authority (*āgama-pramāṇa*).
This refers to the meaning of "receiving instruction.
Third is inference (*anumāna*).
"Inference" means to infer or deduce; it is also a meaning [of the term].
First, it is named according to its meaning; second, as for its essence:
if it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then its essence consists of all phenomena known by both ordinary beings and sages, which are precisely the ultimate and the conventional truths.
Valid cognition through scripture (āgama-pramāṇa) takes the Mahāyāna teachings as its essence,
which has form and consciousness as its nature.

Valid cognition through inference (anumāna-pramāṇa) takes the wisdom of application (prayoga-jñāna), investigative wisdom (vitarka), and wisdom that accords with reality (yathābhūta-jñāna) as its essence.

If one can employ the wisdom of the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the four principles of reasoning (*yukti*), that [wisdom] is by nature solely the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Regarding the fivefold meaning of the term *piṭaka* (storehouse): first, the meaning of "entity" (*tattva*).
Here, "entity" (*tattva*) is a synonym for "reality" (*satya*); it refers to a category or type (*jāti*).
Although all sentient beings grasp many objects, consciousness does not differ from them;
thus, it is established as a name based on the meaning of its substance.
Regarding the two meanings of "cause": the causal cause refers precisely to the conditions and the giving of [the object] to others.
With the practice of the Dharma as the condition,
the three meanings of "arising" (jāti) are established; "arising" refers to that which is capable of producing and growing.
Second, the name is established based on the meaning of functional capacity (*kāritra*).
"Cause" refers to taking [the result] as a cause and acting as a cause;
"arising," however, pertains to the result itself.
Fourth is the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*).
This consciousness is not destroyed in the mundane world nor exhausted upon transcending the world;
this name is established based on its superior significance as characterized by such a form.
The meaning of the five treasuries (*pañca-kośa*):
it clarifies that the substance of this consciousness accumulates merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
this name is established from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Second, the substance (*svabhāva*).
In common usage, the awakened mind (bodhicitta) is understood as the Tathāgatagarbha, which is taken as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the fourfold distinctions of its meaning, it is termed "essence" (*tattva*). As for the term "name":
first, it is the cause of saṃsāra.
That is, it consists of afflictions and karma;
secondly, it is the path to rebirth.
Its essence consists of semblances of form and mind.
Third is the cause of nirvāṇa,
which takes the eightfold noble path as its essence.
Fourth is the fruit of nirvāṇa.
It takes the three bodies and the four kinds of nirvāṇa as its essence.
Regarding the five kinds of impurities:
the first is the false teacher.
That is to say, they take the five aggregates of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the five aggregates of skillful means as their essence.
Second, the heterodox disciples are the same as before.
Third, wrong precepts,
which have the three types of karma— wholesome and unwholesome— as their nature.
Fourth, wrong concentration.
The eight meditative absorptions (dhyāna) constitute its essence.
The five types of false wisdom have as their essence wholesome, unwholesome, or false thought-wisdom and mental action (manas-karman).
This dharma has no written text;
it was transmitted separately as distinct names and characteristics.
There are two types of grasping at the essence: first, the habitual tendencies of the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*).
The first has the seeds of the sense faculties as its essence;
the second has the seeds of the objects of form as its essence.
The commentators take the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) as the essence of the two kinds of grasping (*upādāna*).
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:
"The first refers to grasping based on the faculties of matter and mind."
Second, it is apprehended based on the habitual tendencies of non-conceptual verbal proliferation (*prapañca*).
It consists of two types of mental names and entities: first, that which serves as the basis for their arising.
It takes as its essence the sequential cessation and the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) along with the manas;
it is also called the non-defiled manas.
The second is called the defiled manas.
Because it is characterized by constant association with the four afflictions,
it is established based on its transgressions;
that is, the seventh consciousness constitutes its substance.
The four afflictions are defined by their essential nature: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
"Body" (*kāya*) refers to an accumulation;
"view" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to clarity regarding the object.
The name is derived from the conventional and its referent.
Second is the conceit "I am," where "I" is the object.
Pride is a mental state;
the three types of self-love are also mental states.
These two are named according to their objects and modes of activity.
Fourth is ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is called "ignorance" because it is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*);
it is named after its defect. Its essence is twofold.
They all take the seventh consciousness as their substance (*tattva*).
According to their respective meanings, they are divided into four types; thus, the "drives" (*anuśaya*) may also be enumerated as four.
Regarding the two names and the substance according to the meaning of the three realms: as for the names—
First is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Desire" refers to sexual desire and the desire for edible food.
"Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of the nature of birth.
The three realms of form (*rūpadhātu*).
"Form" refers to the retribution of superior forms and so forth; "desire" refers to desire for form.
The term "realm" (*dhātu*) is the same as before.
These two are named according to their causal meaning.
As for the three formless realms (ārūpyadhātu):
having eliminated desire for form, they arise from the absence of desire for form and are thus called the formless realms.
Names are established based on what is absent. Regarding the two bodies:

if one refers to the realms of desire and form, their substance consists of the five aggregates resulting from the karma of form and the karma of mind, as well as the craving for desire and the delusions regarding form belonging to those respective realms.
The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) takes as its essence the mental karma-afflictions and the four types of mental retribution.
Regarding the two names and one essence for the meanings of *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*: first, they are one in terms of their essence; second, they differ in terms of their various meanings.
The name is derived from its meaning.
Second is *manas* (mind):
it is called mind because it is capable of producing [mental states] in others.
Regarding the three consciousnesses:
that which grasps objects and discerns them is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
These two are designated by their functional efficacy. As for their essence:
If discussed in general terms,
all eight consciousnesses possess this meaning;
however, if discussed specifically:
The seven consciousnesses are called "mind" (*citta*) because they grasp at a self, thereby prolonging birth and death;
the eighth consciousness is called "intellect" (*manas*) because it can serve as the support for the arising of others;
and the sixth consciousness is called "mind" (*citta*) because it can correctly apprehend objects through discernment.
Herein, the ten meanings of the name and essence are as follows. Regarding the "name":
first is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
To act as no obstacle for others is called the dominant condition.
Second, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
that which acts as a condition for an object is called the object-condition.
Third, the characteristic of liberation (*vimukti-lakṣaṇa*).
The substance of the marks is the nature of understanding.
These four function together;
subject and object act in concert to constitute cause and effect.
Fifth, defilement:
it is called "defiled" because it maintains the defiled dharmas of others.
Sixth, the perfuming of karma.
Because it maintains activity, it is called "karmic perfuming" (karma-vāsanā).
It serves as the seventh cause: the causal basis that supports others.
Eighth, the fruit:
that which serves as the produced fruit for others.
Ninth, the path.
In terms of their characteristics, they constitute the five destinies and the ten stages;
in terms of their characteristics, they constitute the three realms and the nine stages. As for their essence:
The functional capacity of the *ālayavijñāna* constitutes its essence (*tattva*).
It is called "essence" because it takes up [objects] and causes them to grow;
thus, the three meanings of "growth" are designated as its essence. First, by means of these ten factors, the mind is made to continue in succession.
This refers to the very functional capacity that serves as the condition for its own continuous growth.
Regarding the three meanings of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: first, the ten dharmas that are emphasized are the cause;
second, this mind is able to sustain the seeds of all phenomena.
That is to say, by means of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), these seeds are formed and subsequently grow.
The fundamental [consciousness] is termed the "conditioning cause" (pratyaya-hetu).
Third is that which grows.
This refers to the karmic retributions of the three realms. Regarding their two natures, there are two [aspects]:
the former takes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its nature, while the latter two are the perfuming factors (*bhāvakadharma*).
Among these, the first is the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of form and mind;
the second is the fruit of the three realms,
which is identical in essence to the preceding three realms.
According to the original record,
the middle one has the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its substance,
while the other two have the perfuming dharmas (*vāsanā-dharma*) as their substance.
In the *Ekottarika-āgama*, there are four names for the essence of consciousness. As for "name" (*nāma*):
it refers to delight (*nandi*), pleasure (*rati*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), habitual practice (*vāsanā*), and attachment (*abhiniveśa*).
Among these, delight, pleasure, and craving are all capable of perfuming (*bhāvaka*).
The World-Honored One, regarding the characteristics of the incomplete teaching, explains the perfuming agent (kṣobhaka) by way of the perfumed object (kṣobhya).
Its essence is no different from what was stated previously;
however, this is spoken from the perspective of that which is derived [from the perfumed].
The essence of joy, pleasure, and so forth is precisely joy, pleasure, and attachment;
these three have the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of greed as their essence.
If one has cultivated the ālayavijñāna, its essence consists of the habitual tendencies of greed, hatred, delusion, and so on.
The second [category] consists of two types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*):
first, craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), which is the craving that arises conditioned by existence;
second, craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
The craving that arises toward the cessation of conditions and retribution is called "craving for non-existence" (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
Both are named after their objects and mental states.
As for their essence, they take the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the mind as their substance.
This refers precisely to the grasping at a self among persons (*pudgala-ātma-grāha*). It pertains to both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Regarding the four inversions (*viparyāsa*), there are two names and two entities: first, the inversion of perceiving purity in what is impure (*aśucau śuci-viparyāsa*).
The thirty-six impure substances are called "impurity.
That which is actually impure is mistakenly reckoned as excellent by those who look toward it.
To reckon that which is not pure as pure is called a perversion (*viparyāsa*).
Second, regarding the misapprehension of suffering as pleasure:
the three realms are all termed "suffering" because they are afflicted by the three types of suffering;
yet, one takes even slight suffering to be pleasure due to craving.
Third is the perversion of taking the impermanent to be permanent:
calculating that which is subject to arising and ceasing as being non-arising and non-ceasing, and thus labeling it "permanent.
Fourth is the perversion of taking the non-self to be a self.
Because it lacks sovereignty, it is called "non-self.
To falsely conceptualize that there is a sovereign presiding deity is what is meant by "self.
Those who are inverted all understand [this] as being contrary to the actual object; thus, it is called "inversion."
The names are established based on their respective meanings; both have two entities as their substance.
Taking the two views and a half as their substance, that is, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), they take delight in acquisition.
The view of annihilationism is half of the view of extremes;
it is the cessation of the impermanent as being permanent.
Regarding the names and essences of the four types of craving: first, craving for food and drink.
Second, clothing;
third, dwellings;
fourth, craving for existence and non-existence.
They are named according to both their mental state and their objective field.
As for their essence, they all have the habitual tendencies of affectionate love as their essence. There is no explicit textual passage regarding the four kinds of rarity;
however, there are three distinct meanings.
First, a distinct intention:
When the Tathāgata originally spoke of the *ālaya* mind, he did so to manifest its meritorious qualities and did not intend to express this particular meaning.
Second, a distinct name.
It merely speaks of the name and does not explain the meaning of consciousness.
There are three distinct meanings:
the subtle object of the Mahāyāna is distinct from that knowledge of suffering and so forth.
The names and entities of the three characteristics: first is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
"Specific" (*sva*) is a term that distinguishes [an entity] from others;
it receives its name based on being contrasted with what is other.
Second is the characteristic of cause.
A cause is a functional capacity,
because it acts as a cause for others.
The designation is established based on its functional capacity.
Regarding the characteristics of the three fruits:
a fruit is termed as such because it is a result that repays another phenomenon capable of perfuming.
The name is established based on the meaning of the fruit.
As for "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa), it refers to the characteristic of phenomena;
phenomena serve as the characteristic.
The name is derived from its meaning. As for its essence (*tattva*):
if one speaks generally, it takes the functional capacity of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its essence;
if one speaks specifically:
The cause takes the meaning of "producing from another" and so forth as its essence;

the effect takes the aspect of "being produced from another" as the essence of the effect's own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); and the preceding cause and effect take their immediate succession as the essence of their own characteristic.
The meaning of the three times has two aspects: name and essence. Regarding the name:
first is the time of preparation (*upāya-kāla*).
That which is not yet the actual performance of an action, but serves as its immediate preceding condition, is called the time of preparation.
Second, regarding the time of actual performance:
the fundamental act of performing the rite is called "actual" (*samyak*);
it is for the sake of the time of actual performance.
The third is called "the time after completion" because it is experienced with a sense of joy and relief following the act;
these names are assigned in mutual relation to one another. Regarding the two entities:
if the three times were identical within a single event, [they would not be distinct].
If it is wholesome, it is wholesome;
if it is unwholesome or neutral, it is unwholesome or neutral respectively.
Its substance consists of the three types of action (karma).
This refers precisely to body, speech, and mind.
If these were not mutually integrated to form a single unity across the preceding and succeeding moments,
then this would be indeterminate, as it would merely follow the description of the preceding phenomena.
Regarding the meaning, names, and substance of the three types of karma— namely, that performed by oneself and so forth—
the first is "that performed by oneself" (*svayaṃkṛta*).
It is called "performed" (*kṛta*) because it takes its own characteristics as its form.
The meaning of "movement" (saṃskāra) is designated based on its characteristics and its function. It consists of two types:
that which performs itself, and that which causes another to act.
The teaching is the condition.
"Other" has the meaning of being mutually defined by form.
From this mutual definition and its meaning, the name arises.
Third is the function of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).
Consciousness follows after the good, evil, and other such deeds of others;
this is termed "following" (*anu*).
Joy (*prīti*) is the arising of mental pleasure;
it is named as such because it proceeds exclusively from the mind. Regarding its essence:
whether performed by oneself or taught to others, when considered generally, [it is of one nature].
It has as its nature the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
If it is performed through sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), it has only the karma of mind as its nature;
however, it may also extend to the two karmas of body and speech.
The three [types of] dependent origination regarding name and substance:
as for "name," first is dependent origination by way of intrinsic nature;
the term "self" (sva) refers to "substance" (svabhāva).
The cause of nature may also have the meaning of "not changing.
Condition (*pratyaya*) has the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*).
Birth is the fruit;
it is named according to its nature as both cause and fruit.
Second, there are the desirable and the undesirable.
Wholesome retribution that accords with one's desires is called "loved";
unwholesome retribution that opposes one's desires is called "unloved.
These names are derived from their meaning.
Third, regarding "appropriation" (*upabhoga*):
consciousness is able to receive objects, which is termed "grasping the object" (*viṣayagrahaṇa*);
