this is designated as "appropriation" based on the functional capacity of the mind. As for its "substance" (*svabhāva*):
Its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) has the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as its essence.
Its aspect of the desirable and undesirable has the five aggregates (skandha), comprising both the preparatory means and the karmic fruition, as its essence.
Its aspect of experience has the six consciousnesses (ṣaḍvijñāna) as its essence.
The two kinds of birth-body (janmakāya) are its essence and substance: first, the birth-body born in the fortunate realms;
second, the birth-body born in the miserable realms.
Virtue and non-virtue are their causes.
The Way (mārga) has the meaning of "penetrating and giving birth.
The retributive fruit is called the "birth-body" (janman-kāya).
It takes "relying upon" as its primary meaning; it is named according to its cause, its fruit, and its underlying significance.
The substance is identical to what is loved and what is not loved.
"Substance" refers to the three types of karma; as for "name," it refers to the first: sinful karma.
The bitter fruits of the three miserable realms are termed "offenses" (pāpa),
named after their transgressions.
Second are meritorious karmas (puṇya-karma).
Karma that is skillful in its essence and capable of producing pleasant results is called merit (*puṇya*);
it is named according to its functional meaning.
Third is immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*).
The fruit obtained cannot be shifted as to its level (bhūmi) or its realm of rebirth (gati).

This is because, for example, the unwholesome karma of the desire realm may result in the karma of humans or devas being experienced in the evil destinies; therefore, it is not called "fixed" (niyata).
Regarding the two entities designated by their functions:
the function of transgression takes the body, speech, and mind as its entity;
the function of merit takes the three types of wholesome karma—body, speech, and mind—of the desire realm as its entity.

The functional activity of immovability (aniñjya-karma) has as its essence both the simultaneous concentration of mental volition and the non-informative action (avijñapti) associated with the seven branches of bodily and vocal discipline.
Regarding the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination, there are two names and two essences: first, ignorance (avidyā).
It is not established by anything other than this. Second, regarding "formations" (*saṃskāra*):
they are called formations because they initiate and produce subsequent effects.
The three consciousnesses.
"Discriminating" is the definition of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
These two [terms] are established as names based on their function.
The fourth is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
"Name" (*nāma*) refers generally to all mental factors (*cittadharma*);
"form" (*rūpa*) refers to that which resembles form and so forth.
Names are established based on both meaning and substance.
Regarding the "six" and "five" in the term *ṣaḍāyatana*: "six" is a number.
It enters into this meaning because the mind enters and exits through it; thus,
it receives its name from the sense of "counting."
Sixth, contact (*sparśa*);
that is, mental contact with objects.
Seventh, sensation (*vedanā*).
The apprehension of an object is called feeling (*vedanā*);
it is also an activity (*karman*).
There are eight types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The defiled mind that clings to objects is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
this is a name derived from its meaning.
These three [defilements] are named according to their functional meanings.
The nine appropriations (*upādāna*).
Because the preceding craving (*tṛṣṇā*) further intensifies and gives rise to karma, it is called "appropriation.
This name is derived from its functional meaning.
The tenth is "existence" (bhava).
That is to say, present karma that is capable of obtaining a future fruit is called existence;
it is named after its result.
Eleventh, arising (*jāti*):
this refers to the arising of new sense faculties (*indriya*), which is called "arising" because it is the fruit;
it is named after its fruit.
Twelfth is old age and death.
The deterioration and transformation of the faculties is called "old age";
the transition and departure of consciousness is called "death."
The two entities are named according to their past [causes].
In general, they take afflictions, karma, and retribution as their nature.
Within this, the distinction is as follows:
In the preceding section on dependent origination,
ignorance is an affliction and volitional formations are karma.
The five beginning with consciousness are maturation;
in the subsequent [section on] dependent origination,
craving and grasping are afflictions.
There is this karma;
birth, old age, and death are its retribution.
To speak of it in general terms:
Ignorance, craving, and grasping are afflictions;
volitional formations and existence are karma;
the remaining seven are retribution.
At that time, all distinctions pertain to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is included within the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the meaning of the three paths: this refers to the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).
That which defiles the pure mind is called affliction (*kleśa*).
Because it can produce karma, it is called the path (*mārga*).
It is named according to its transgression and its function.
There are two paths of action (*karmapatha*).
That which is performed is called "action" (*karman*);
because it can produce retribution, it is called a "path" (*patha*).
Third, the "paths" (mārga).
They are called "retribution" (vipāka) because they result from prior causes;
they are called "paths" because they are capable of producing afflictions (kleśa) and karma (karman).
The two bodies are designated according to their meaning and function:
the body of afflictions has the habitual tendencies of the mind as its essence,
while the body of karma has the three types of action— of body, speech, and mind— as its nature.
The retribution-body (vipākakāya) takes the five aggregates as its substance.
Regarding the meanings and names of the three delusions, such as ignorance (*ajñāna*):
first, "ignorance" refers to ordinary beings who, due to their lack of clear understanding, are called ignorant.
Thus, there is no name other than "feeling.
Second is "knowledge through doubt," which takes the very essence of doubt as its name.
Third, inverted cognition.
To act in opposition to the correct principle is called "inversion.
For the mind to grasp with firm resolve is called "cognition."
The "entity" (tǐ) is designated by its functional meaning:
ignorance refers to the four dull underlying tendencies (anuśaya),
and doubt refers to the underlying tendency of doubt.
Perversion consists of the five false views;
collectively, these comprise the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*).
They may also be said to pertain to three types of persons: ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), bodhisattvas, and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
There are two kinds of views:
first, the view of inequality;
and second, the four views, which are the view of extremes, the view of permanence and self, the adherence to precepts and rituals, and the adherence to views.
Because the principle of cause and effect is not established when the two [factors] are unequal and do not meet, and because they are always perceived as being fundamental,
these are designated by names derived from their faulty meanings.
Furthermore, according to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), a cause is a fixed cause and cannot function as an effect.
The fruit is the very fruit of meditative concentration and cannot serve as its cause;
therefore, it is not equal.
Second, there would be no cause.
This is precisely wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The mind that clings to non-existence destroys the principle of the true cause; this is called "causelessness" (*ahetuka*).
It is named after that which is non-existent.
The twenty-five principles (*tattva*) of Sāṃkhya are analyzed according to five meanings.
First, because the whole exists apart from its parts,
and the parts are transformations (*vikāra*).
The first is always the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The second is because the end implies the beginning:
transformation is the end.
The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the root.
Since greed, hatred, and delusion exist within the derivative branches, one knows that the intrinsic nature also exists therein.
Third, it is because the thing possesses functional capacity.
Phenomena are phenomena;
they can function and can produce all things.
It is because of the existence of the functional entity that it can be thus;
"entity" (tattva) is synonymous with "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva).
This constitutes the fourfold distinction between cause and effect.
The cause is the self-nature;
the effect is the transformed effect.
Fifth, by means of the discrimination between the existence and non-existence of the three [realms].
Because one enters into the primal nature (*prakṛti*) through the transformation [of the evolutes], there is non-discrimination regarding the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
Primal nature is the root;
from primal nature, intellect (*buddhi*) is produced.
From intellect (buddhi) arises the I-principle (ahaṃkāra);
from the I-principle arise the five subtle elements (tanmātras);
and from the five subtle elements, the five gross elements (mahābhūtas) are formed.
The five great elements (mahābhūta) constitute the eleven faculties.
The five subtle potentials (tanmātra) are the five sense objects.
The five great elements consist of the four great elements plus space.

To the eleven faculties and the five faculties such as the eye, add the hands, feet, mouth, anus, male and female organs, along with the faculty of mind (*manas*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Adding the faculty of "I know" (*ahaṃ vedayāmīndriya*) makes twenty-five.
Sixth, grasping at names as substantial entities. "Name" refers to:
first, the calculation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The term "self" (*sva*) signifies "entity" (*bhāva*).
The term "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the cause;
it is named according to its essence and function.
Second is "past action" (*pūrvakṛta*).
When an event has passed away, it is termed "past" (*atīta*);
that which is past and capable of being designated is called a "name.
A name is established according to its meaning and function.
Third is the transformation of mastery (*vaśitā-vikurvaṇa*).
Mastery refers to the dharma of retribution;
it is called mastery because it accords with the mind.
The alteration of color, form, and name constitutes a transformation;
that which was non-existent suddenly acquires a name through transformation.
Thus, names are established according to their predominant functions.
There are four kinds of eightfold self-mastery (*vaśitā*).
Unimpeded activity is called mastery;
that which possesses mastery is due to the self (*ātman*).
The meaning of the essence itself constitutes the name.
There are five kinds of non-existence (*abhāva*):
when a perverted mind takes a ruined phenomenon as its object, it is termed "non-existence."
The "cause" refers precisely to the cause of that which is non-existent;
it is designated by way of mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
There are six types of grasping at a self as an agent and an experiencer.
The "self" is this mind;
it is reckoned as the essence of the sovereign spirit.
The "agent" is that which I am able to act as the cause.
The "appropriator" (upādātr) is the act of appropriation; the appropriator is itself the "self" (ātman).
This is designated according to its essence and its function. Regarding the two essences:
as for the essential nature, it consists of the view of permanence, which is a portion of the view of extremes, and the view of self, along with the adherence to precepts and observances.
The latent tendency of wrong view previously formed may also have the nature of adherence to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) or adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
In the case of the eternalist view of a self-existent creator (īśvara), there is both adherence to rules and observances and also adherence to views.
The eight types of "mastery over self" (aiśvarya) have the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi) and the attachment to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) as their essence;
they have these false views as their cause.

The [notions of] the self as agent (kartṛ) and experiencer (bhoktṛ) have the four views—the false view, the view of a self, the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and the attachment to precepts and observances—as their essence.
In summary, its essence consists of the five views and twenty-five principles;
this is the Sāṃkhya interpretation adopted by the Ṛṣi Kapila.
Arising from meditative concentration, one forms this attachment.
This is the mind of affliction belonging to the stage of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Because one is not aware of anything beyond eighty thousand eons, it is called "darkness" (*mīṅ*).
That which is delusion and ignorance is called "darkness" (ming).
From darkness arises the "Great" (mahat); that which takes karma as its basis is the Great.
The state of being born and receiving existence is named the Great.
The *Śataśāstra* defines awakening (*buddhi*).
When awakening arises, conceit (*māna*) follows; this is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Between the two aggregates (*skandha*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises.
The *Śataśāstra* calls this the "mind of self.
From this self arise two things: namely, form and mind.
Form has twenty-one varieties.
The five sense objects, the five great elements, the five faculties, the five karmas, and the mind as the twenty-first constitute the group of equality.
There are three types of mental factors:
defiled, coarse, and dark.
Including the previous ones, there are twenty-four.
Adding the faculty of discernment (*vijñāna*) and the mind-faculty (*manas*), they become twenty-six.
Since the male and female faculties do not coexist in a single person, it is said that there are twenty-five.
The essence of the eight masteries is as follows: first, mastery over the subtle and the most subtle;
second, mastery over the large and the greatest;
third, pervasive arrival.
Fourth, the power of acting according to one's will;
fifth, the power of being unattached;
sixth, the power of transformation.
Seventh, it is eternally unchanging;
eighth, it is pure and free from sorrow. Its essence is identical to that which takes "self" as its essence;
thus, it is divided into eight aspects.
Second, the nature of the two types of seeds. Regarding "names":
first, external seeds.
As for their nature, those that are non-sentient are termed "external."
The name is derived from its meaning.
Second, regarding the internal seeds:
their substance is the mind of the sentient path, and thus they are called "internal."
The name is derived from its meaning;
it is generally termed "seed" (*bīja*).
As for its essence, the name is derived from its functional meaning.
The internal [seeds] take the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of matter and mind as their essence;
they may also have karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and retribution as their nature.
The external seeds take the four sense objects—matter and so forth—as their essence.
The meanings and names of the two causes that produce [phenomena] are as follows: regarding "name," first is the producing cause (*janana-hetu*).
It is called "producing" because it directly brings about the manifestation of the result.
That which is produced is called the "fruit" (phala),
and that which produces is called the "cause" (hetu).
These names are derived from their functional capacity and their results.
Second, the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
That which is sustained by the power of other worlds is called "projecting.
Both are named according to their functional capacity (*śakti*). Second, as for their essential nature (*svabhāva*):

If it is of the nature of the karmic seeds that serve as the projecting cause for internal arising, then "arising" (*jāti*) refers simply to the taking up of what was non-existent as a retribution so that it comes to exist;
it persists thereafter without perishing due to being projected by karma. Therefore, the treatise says:
The seed has two capacities:
first, the capacity to produce;
second, the capacity to project.
If external seeds take the four objects— color and the other three forms— as their substance,
there are three distinctions:
first, the basis.
The various faculties, such as the eye and so forth, are each distinct and different;
they are called "bases" (āśraya) because they give rise to consciousness.
They are designated by name according to their meaning and their functional capacity.
Second, each [consciousness] individually takes its object.
Each consciousness apprehends its respective object; because the consciousness arises in distinction from that object, the object is termed "object" (*viṣaya*).
This name is derived from its meaning.
The three— distinct vitarka, distinct vicāra, and distinct saṃjñā—
are all differences in the application of attention (manasikāra).
Vitarka and vicāra are the preliminary application of attention.
Discriminative thought (*vikalpa*) is also the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that apprehends the specific characteristics of objects;
it is named according to its functional meaning.
Regarding the four conditions, their names and essential natures are as follows: first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That which is capable of producing a fruit is called a cause (*hetu*).
Because it functions as a cause, it is termed a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This name is derived from its functional efficacy and its underlying meaning.
Second is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
That which takes a dominant dharma as its condition is called the dominant condition.
Third is the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The preceding mind being the cause for the subsequent successive dharma is called the condition as immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya).
It is named after its effect.
The fourth is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
That which is produced is a mental factor (*cittadharma*).
Because it serves as a condition for its object, it is called the "object-condition" (*ālambanapratyaya*);
thus, it receives the name of two conditions.
Regarding the name derived from its meaning, as for its substance (*tattva*):
it refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) in which the seeds within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), being of the same nature as the mind, directly produce dharmas.
Alternatively, one may simply take the seeds themselves [to be the substance].
The immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) has both matter (rūpa) and mind (citta) as its substance.
The dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) encompasses all phenomena,
with the sole exception of itself.
The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is likewise.
Regarding the two types of predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), as for their names and entities:
first is the inseparable predominant condition.
Because they arise simultaneously,
they are named according to their meaning;
thus, there are only two.
That is to say, "name" has the meaning of mutual dependence. Regarding the "two substances":
all phenomena, such as form and mind, constitute the substance.
Just as ignorance gives rise to volitional formations through two powers, suffering and so forth are inseparable; thus, they exist only within the path of cultivation.
Just as it is with ignorance in relation to itself, so it is with all other phenomena.
There are three principles: first, the principle of purification.
Second, the category of impurity;
third, that which accords with reason,
which arises from the karma of ethical discipline.
That which is of a nature with outflows (*sāsrava*) is termed "impure" (*aśubha*);
this is a designation based on its defects.
That which is of a nature without outflows (*anāsrava*) and the eight meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) that possess outflows are termed "pure" (*śubha*).
It is designated by way of its freedom from faults.
If one establishes it as the *ālaya*, it accords with the principles of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth.
It is designated by way of its meaning. As for its essence:
If one establishes the doctrinal meaning by relying on the three [wisdoms],
its essence consists of the wisdoms arising from hearing and reflection;
as for the phenomena upon which it relies:
The category of the impure (*aśubha*) has afflictions, karma, and its retribution as its essence.
The category of the pure (*śubha*) has the three types of wisdom—derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, both mundane and supramundane—as its essence.
That which accords with principle has conditioned and unconditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta* and *asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as its essence.
If one takes the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as the essence, it has the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its nature;
if one takes cause and effect as the essence, they have the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as their nature.
Regarding the meaning of the term "essence" (*tattva*) in the context of the great and small afflictions (*kleśa*): first, the great affliction.
Second, regarding the two minor afflictions (*upakleśa*):
"minor" and "major" are relative designations; "affliction" refers to their fault.
They are named according to their meaning and their faults. Second, regarding their essence (*svabhāva*): [text continues].
The great delusions take the ten proclivities as their essence,
because they possess five characteristics;
the minor delusions take the envelopments and stains as their essence.

Because it does not possess five characteristics, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) differs from the sixth and seventh consciousnesses in three respects: first, its grasping and maintenance are uninterrupted;
for, in terms of its appropriation and maintenance of the retribution-body (*vipākadeha*), there is not even a single moment’s interval in which it does not maintain them.
Second, it universally sustains all the sense faculties;
this clarifies that this consciousness does not sustain only a single faculty.
Third, its essence is the retributive neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*).

Because they serve as the supporting basis for the production of fruits, they are both designated by names derived from their functional capacities. As for their substance (*tattva*), it is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) without distinction;
the four nutriments (*āhāra*) are the names, while their substance is as follows.
First is the food of edible morsels,
so named according to its characteristic.
Second is the food of contact.
The food of contact (*sparśāhāra*) exists because of the encounter with sense objects;
the food of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) exists because of intentional seeking.
These two are named according to their functional activity.
As for the fourth, the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*): it is called "consciousness" because it consists of mind and cognition.
The name is derived from its essence and function;
it is generally termed "nutriment" (āhāra) because the name is derived from its functional capacity.
Because they are able to bring about the production [of beings], there are two entities:
morsel food has as its essence the consciousness of similar form;
contact has as its essence the six consciousnesses.
Volition (*cetanā*) has volitional thought as its essence; seeking food has the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as its essence;
and nutriment (*āhāra*) has the *ālayavijñāna* as its essence.
Regarding the four meanings of "taking birth," their essence is as follows: first, it takes defilement (*kleśa*) as its root.
The intermediate state (antarābhava) has the mental consciousness as its essence;
the two types of distraction also have the mental consciousness as their essence.
The former is distinguished by its grasping of the three genders.
Now, to summarize and distinguish them:
third, they have as their nature the three types of karma—meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable—which have residual effects;
fourth, they have retribution as their substance.

Since this ālayavijñāna constitutes the substance of retribution, the dharmas of the form realm (rūpadhātu) and the desire realm (kāmadhātu) possess four kinds of distinctions in their names and substances: first, coarseness and subtlety.
Because the mind in the desire realm lacks meditative concentration, it is coarse.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) is subtle because it possesses meditative concentration (samādhi);
secondly, because there is a difference between movement and stillness;
and thirdly, because there is a difference in the cultivation of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
The four types of bondage and their deliverance differ;
these are named according to their functional capacity and their characteristics. As for their two natures:
the desire realm has the wisdoms of hearing and reflection as its nature.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) has hearing, reflection, and cultivation as its essence.
Right view is designated as "essence" in the sense that it possesses two causes: first, hearing from others;
this is designated by way of its meaning and its object.
Second, regarding "correct mental attention" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*):
it is named after the mental faculty that functions toward the meaning. Second, as for its essence:
its essence consists of hearing and reflection.
Regarding the supramundane [mind]: Question.
Since the master of the treatise has never produced a supramundane mind from the outset, how can it become the seed of the supramundane? Answer.
It is established by way of two causes and conditions,
which differ from that school's position.
The first is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
It is understood that this Mahāyāna teaching flows from the most pure *dharmadhātu*;
therefore, one knows that because its dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) differs from those [other vehicles], it enables the attainment of the supramundane.
In the Hīnayāna, it is not understood that the teachings arise from the fundamental nature;
for this reason, they differ.
Second, the causal conditions differ.
In the Hīnayāna, the existence of the three time periods as substantial entities is established; thus,
the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the world cannot become the cause for transcending the world,
and one does not arise from that teaching [to do so].

If one considers the thesis established by our Mahāyāna, even the ten wholesome actions of ordinary beings within the human and celestial realms can act as causes to produce the latencies of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*). Question:
If mundane minds can cultivate supramundane dharmas such that they are able to give rise to supramundane dharmas, [is this not possible]?
Question: Since the ten wholesome paths of action and so forth are fundamentally not practiced as supramundane understandings, how can they lead to transcendence of the world? Answer:
There are two reasons why these can give rise to supramundane dharmas.
First, regarding these ten wholesome courses of action, by virtue of what phenomena do they arise?
They arise through the power of the *tathāgatagarbha*;

because their causal basis is not distinct [from that of worldly dharmas], they are able to give rise to supramundane dharmas. Second, this is the intended meaning behind the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teaching of these ten wholesome courses of action.
Desire gives rise to supramundane dharmas for sentient beings;
it is by virtue of these two meanings that one is able to produce supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"All virtuous practices performed are none other than the great, pure, and pure skillful means;
the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle is likewise so."
The four dharmas beginning with faith are as follows:
first, faith and delight in the Mahāyāna;
this is the seeking of joy and the desire for that joy.
The Mahāyāna is the object.
It is named according to the mind and its object.
There are two types of Prajñā.
The third is the samādhi of the vessel of space.
The vessel of space is the object;
samādhi is meditative concentration.
The first four [immeasurables] are named according to their objective essence (*ālambana-svabhāva*);
the latter two are named according to their functional capacity (*kāritra*). The former two are the essence.
Faith takes the mind of wisdom derived from hearing as its essence;
Prajñā takes the knowledge of non-self as its essence;
and the Samādhi of Space takes the concentration on the three natures of non-existence as its essence.
Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) takes the meditative concentration on the activities of great compassion as its essence.
In terms of wisdom, it is the wisdom of application (prayoga-jñāna).
Regarding the names for its essence and its modes: as for the "names": [The text continues: ...the name is... [as per the source].
First is pure virtue (*śuddhaguṇa*).
The elimination of base and evil is termed "pure attainment" (*śuddhilābha*);
that is, it is named after the departure from faults.
Second, regarding "self":
that which possesses sovereignty is called "self";
this is a designation based on its function.
The intrinsic nature of the three kinds of happiness is tranquility and stillness, which is termed "happiness.
It may also be termed "happiness" because it brings satisfaction;
thus, the name is established based on its functional meaning.
The four are "constant.
Their essence is without abiding or cessation, which is termed "constant.
Furthermore, there are also four kinds.
All are named after their departure from faults.
As for their essence: speaking generally, they all share the *ālayavijñāna* as their essential nature.
It may also take the dharma-body as its nature.
The fivefold dharma-body is defined by its essence: the body of precepts (*śīla-kāya*).
To prevent what is non-virtuous is "precept."
The body of concentration:
concentration is the cessation of distraction.
The body of wisdom.
Discernment is wisdom (*prajñā*).
These three are named according to their functions.
Liberation (*vimukti*).
It is named "receiving" because it is free from faults.
To know and see the body is called "knowing," which refers to the arising of the mind with respect to an object that can be perceived.
"Clear understanding" (prajñapti) is called "vision" (darśana).
It receives its name from its functional meaning;
as for its essence (svabhāva), if we speak generally:
Thus, they take non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) as their essence. To discuss them individually:
the essence of ethical discipline (*śīla*) consists of the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-koṭi-viśuddha-śīla*);
the essence of the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) takes non-conceptual wisdom as its essence.
Liberation (vimukti) has as its essence the absence of doubt regarding the extremes of morality, concentration, and so forth, or the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Knowledge and vision (jñānadarśana) have as their essence subsequent knowledge (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
Among supramundane [wisdoms], the three types of wisdom (prajñā) are designated by the term "essence."
The first is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Hearing" refers to the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) apprehending a preceding sound through various conditions;
this is called "hearing. "Wisdom" refers to the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) performing discrimination; this is termed "wisdom."
Second is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*):
settling the mind and examining with discernment is called reflection.
Third is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
The meaning of "cultivation" (bhāvanā) is the meaning of "intensification.
Wisdom of cultivation is not wisdom of hearing or reflection;
it is called "cultivation" because it arises from hearing and the other [stages].
The wisdoms of hearing and so forth are named after their respective causes;
they are two in substance, yet three in wisdom.
They differ in that they all take as their intrinsic nature the mental factor of wisdom (prajñā) functioning within the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Regarding the three types of wholesome states, such as the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), there are two names for their essence. As for the names:
first is the "factor conducive to liberation.
Liberation is the fruit.
The stage of penetration (*prativedhabhāgīya*) is the cause, because it serves as the causal portion for the fruit.
Second is the stage of penetration.
The mind that penetrates and realizes this principle is itself the fruit;
its function is not different from what preceded it.
These two names are established based on the meanings of "fruit" and "cause."
The third is the Chapter on Thorough Penetration (*praveśa*).
"Thorough penetration" means to realize and perceive the principle (*tattva*) such that neither subject nor object is perceived; this is what is meant by "thorough penetration.
It carries the sense of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
"Chapters" (p'in) refers to their distinct classifications;
thus, names are established based on their functional significance. Regarding the "two bodies":
as for the two preceding [bodies], their primary substance takes the two types of wisdom—namely, that derived from hearing and that derived from reflection—as their essential nature.
The former is hearing;
the latter is reflection.
They also both take the nature of the two wisdoms—reflection and cultivation—as their essence.
This refers specifically to mental action (manas-karman).
If one includes its preceding and subsequent attendants,
then it has the nature of all three actions— body, speech, and mind.
If one takes the direct penetration as the primary focus,
then it consists solely of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) and has mental action (*manas-karman*) alone as its essence.
This is the case once one has emerged from the supramundane mind.
It takes the three karmas of body, speech, and mind as its essence.
Regarding "hearing," there are three meanings for its name and essence: first, the equipment for hearing;
by means of sounds, names, phrases, and so forth, it brings to completion the wisdom of hearing and the auditory consciousness.
The name is derived from its function according to its meaning.
Second, the essence of hearing;
hearing is the function.
The essence is the meaning;
it is named according to its meaning and function.
Third is the fruit of hearing.
This refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and the Dharma-gates understood through hearing; both are accomplished by means of hearing.
Since the result is designated by the name of its cause, these two constitute the essence.
The function of the accumulation of hearing has sound, form, and consciousness as its essence.
The essence of hearing has the apprehending consciousness as its essence.
The fruit of hearing has the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the associated dharma-gates as its essence.
Regarding the two names for the four kinds of counteractives (*pratipakṣa*), they are derived from the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanatory Treatise).
First is the counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*).
"Abandonment" (*pra*) and "extinction" (*hāṇa*) refer to the power of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*) which suppresses the afflictions.
Second is the antidote of distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*).
Distancing refers to that which causes the obstacles to distancing through hearing and reflection.
These two are designated by names derived from the function of their respective remedies.
Third is the antidote to decay.
Decay refers to the power of hearing and reflection causing karma to lose its functional efficacy; this is termed "decay.
The designation based on this meaning may likewise be applied [to the term "antidote"].
The fourth is the antidote subsumed by reliance.
Reliance refers to the mental capacity of the practitioner;
subsumption refers to the great compassionate mind of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
These names are derived from the subject and object of cognition.
As for the second [category], the name is established based on the functional capacity of the path as its antidote. Regarding their essential nature:
if one discusses the first [category], it consists of the afflictions, karma, and the retribution thereof, which are the objects to be countered by the view.
The second is retribution in the next life;
the third is subsequent retribution, consisting of afflictions and karma;

the fourth consists of taking as its essence the difficulties among the eight unfavorable conditions (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa), such as being born before or after a Buddha, having impaired intelligence, being born blind, and so forth, as well as the long-lived heavens of the northern continent.

If one takes that which counteracts [the afflictions] as its function, it consists of the hearing and reflection of those from the stage of the ten faiths upward; it may also include cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Regarding the four meanings of "much learning" (*bahuśruta*), there are two aspects: name and substance. First, the cause of much learning.
That is to say: first, taking the bodhicitta as its essence;
second, the reliance upon extensive learning, which takes the five aggregates (skandhas) of the spiritual friends—Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—as its essence;
third, the purification of extensive learning.
It has the six pāramitās as its essence.
The four fruits of extensive learning have the two types of wisdom—
the fundamental wisdom and the subsequently attained wisdom— as their essence.
Regarding the existence of mind within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*,
it is explained that there is mind within the meditative absorption of cessation.
This is the position established by Vasumitra.
The master of śāstras, Ghoṣaka, challenges it with the argument that contact and so forth arise from the conjunction of the three.
He cites the case of an arhat experiencing sensation without giving rise to craving as his illustrative example.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*:
Question:
At the time of entering that meditative absorption...
If the mental factors are gradually extinguished,
why does the Blessed One speak only of the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling"?
Answer:
The Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that there is mind within the attainment of cessation;
they speak as follows.
When entering that meditative absorption,
because only these two factors cease,
the absorption is a mental formation dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
It is called the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
As for the term "attainment" (*samāpatti*): because the four great elements remain unmoving when one has accomplished the meditative state through bodily application, it is called "attainment.
Question:
What is the difference between meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and cessation (*nirodha*)? Answer:
Cessation lasts for only a single moment, whereas meditative absorption is a long-term continuity.
Question:
For what reason is it called only the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling"?
Answer:
Within the mental factors, there are two types: those that are faculties and those that are not faculties.
Having explained feeling, the faculties have been explained;
having explained perception, that which is not of the nature of a faculty has been explained.
Second, the definition and nomenclature of the two mindless states. Regarding the names:
first is the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), which is named according to its absence of conceptualization.
Second is the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). "Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the functional power of the concentration;
"concentration" (*samāpatti*) has the meaning of being immovable.
The names are established based on their function and meaning. Regarding the two natures (*dvaya-svabhāva*), there is no definitive textual passage from the Mahāyāna;
they are discussed here by way of their meaning.
Because it is sought through the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) of a bodhisattva,
and because the mental factors associated with wisdom do not arise, it is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) constitutes the essence of this meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Since the state of non-ideation is also sought after by the minds of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*),
it likewise takes this non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) essence; this point must further be investigated.
The Names and Meanings of the Ten Faults: 1. The fault of the definition:
it fails to establish the mind, such that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not achieved.
2. The fault of generating misconceptions regarding characteristics and objects.
If the mind is established, there is the fault of the mental object arising from the conditions of sensory objects.
Third is the fault of being associated with wholesome roots:
when the mind is established, wholesome roots such as non-attachment necessarily arise and become associated with the mind.
Fourth, there is the fault that it would not correspond with the unwholesome or neutral [states],
because if this were mind, one could not establish the factors of the unwholesome or neutral stages as being absent.
Fifth, there is the fault that perception and feeling would arise [independently].
If there were necessarily mental factors in meditative concentration, there would be the fault of the arising of sensation (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā).
This is because of the fault that contact (sparśa) arises from the conjunction of the six [bases].
If there were necessarily a mind in meditative concentration, then there must be the three factors—the sense organ, the object, and consciousness—in conjunction; thus, contact would arise.
Seventh, the fault that the cessation of perception does not entail the cessation of feeling:

this contradicts the Noble One’s teaching on the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*), because the Buddha taught that both perception and feeling are absent therein.
Eighth, the fault that mental attention (*manasikāra*) would give rise to faith and other [wholesome factors].
If one posits that the mind exists, then mental factors such as faith must necessarily arise together with it;
thus, there is the fault of violating the principle that the nine [mental factors] can be separated from what they accompany.
Furthermore, if one posits that the mind exists but does not admit the existence of perception and feeling, there is the fault of contradicting the inseparability of the faculty and its objects.
The fault that the ten established positions are not uniform is as follows:
because inhalation and exhalation are not the universal concomitants (sarvatraga) of the body,
one may analogously argue that mental factors such as feeling and perception are the universal concomitants of the mind-king (citta-rāja).

Because this meaning is not analogous [to the previous case], the characteristics and entities of the two types of understanding are as follows: first, that which is with conceptualization (*savikalpa*).
"With" (*sa*) means that the mind possesses a superior capacity, and thus it is termed "with."
The functional power of existence is called "discrimination";
it is named after its functional activity.
The two [types of non-conceptual knowledge] are without discrimination.
That which has slight power and function is called "non-existent.
The phenomena that are non-existent are called "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*).
As for the essence [of these], it is named based on what is other than non-existence.
Non-conceptual [cognition] has the six consciousnesses as its substance;
conceptual [cognition] uses only the mental consciousness as its substance.
These four types of indeterminate [states] are designated by their substance.
This is the doctrine of the Saṃmitīya school: that which is termed "name" (nāman) is of one type— obscured-neutral—
and its essence is the nature of affliction (kleśa).
That which obscures the noble path is called "obscured" (*nivṛta*);
it is named after its transgression.
The other two are the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
It is not of the nature of delusion;
because it does not obscure the Noble Path, it is called "unobscured" (*anivṛta*).
It is named from the standpoint of its being free from fault.
The three natures are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
"Self" (*sva*) is a term used to distinguish [the nature] from others;
"nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to its essence (*tattva*).
They are designated according to their characteristics and forms.
Within their intrinsic nature, they are divided into four types:
those born of retribution, those of deportment, those of transformation, and those of craftsmanship.
The fourth is the truly indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Its essence is not conditioned; that which is characterized by arising and ceasing is called "real" (*tattva*) in terms of its meaning, and thus it is so named.
It is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) because it is not defined as either wholesome or unwholesome;
furthermore, it cannot be defined as having results such as suffering or pleasure.
The substance [of this consciousness] is named according to its function;
it takes the seven consciousnesses as its nature.
Furthermore, the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*) of the two upper realms is also included.
The second [category] of the indeterminate takes the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as its essence;
the third takes the four types of indeterminate states, such as retribution (vipāka), as its essence;
and the fourth takes the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as its essence.
There are two kinds of what is called "name" (*nāman*): first, the name as verbal expression, which is designated based on its substance;
second, the name as mental conceptualization.
Contemplation is the functional power of this mind;
it is named according to its activity. Regarding the two entities, there are two reasons for their distinction:
first, both take sound as their essential nature.
As the treatise states: "Because both take sound as their basis.
Question:
As for the term "contemplation" (思惟), how can it be considered sound?
Answer:
This mental discrimination is called "mind" (manas), and it is also called "sound" (śabda).
Second, when we say that sound is the fundamental [nature] here, this does not mean it is the essential substance (svabhāva).
This refers to the meaning of "cause.
Verbal expression has sound as its essence;
contemplation has the mind as its essence.
Question:
If that is so, why is it said that they are alike in having sound as their basis?
Answer:
To say that "speech is the basis" means that it is the name for the act of reflection;
because meaning first begins to be differentiated by means of speech, speech is said to be the basis.
He asked again:
"If that is so, what are the seven consciousnesses?
He replied:
The seven consciousnesses assist the mental consciousness (manovijñāna),
and the mental consciousness also exerts power over the seven consciousnesses.
If this were not so, [the system would fail].
The seven consciousnesses cannot cure the seven consciousnesses;
since there is the meaning of "curing," it is clear that there must also be the meaning of "sustaining."
Because there is material support (*upadhi*), there is the mental state of distance; sound is the basis.
That form and mind arise in succession is the doctrine of the Saṃmitīya school.
The prior form arises as the sequential condition for the subsequent form;
the mind is likewise.
They reckon this to be the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Now, the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is refuted as being untenable.
The eleven types of characteristics are the names and entities of the faculties (*indriya*). Regarding "names":
first, there is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Mountains, rivers, and so forth are called "common characteristics" (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) because they are shared by all beings.
Second are the "uncommon characteristics" (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*):
internal retributions, sentient states, and paths are each not shared with others, and thus are called uncommon characteristics.
The third is the "possessor of sensation," which refers to the sentient path of experiencing.
The fourth is the "essence of non-sensation."
Inanimate paths, being devoid of awareness, are called "unappropriated.
Regarding the five characteristics of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness):
within the phenomena of principle and fact, the functional capacity of the mind is termed *dausthulya*.
Sixth is subtlety and lightness;
because the mind possesses functional capacity regarding both principle and phenomena, it is called subtle and light.
Seventh is the characteristic of being possessed of sensation.
When a karmic dharma receives its retribution and is immediately exhausted, it is called "with reception" (sopādāna).
Eight [types of dharma] are "without reception" (anupādāna).
Alternatively, when a dharma receives its retribution and further increases, it is called "without reception."
Ninth is the characteristic of simile.
To draw a comparison is called a "simile" (upamā);
to illustrate the profound by means of the proximate is called a "metaphor" (dṛṣṭānta).
10. "Possessing characteristics" refers to defiled phenomena that have not yet been impaired by their antidotes; thus they are called "possessing characteristics.
11. "Not possessing characteristics" refers to defiled phenomena that have been impaired by the Path; thus they are called "not possessing characteristics."
Regarding the two aspects of essence, there are both general and specific types.
First, as for the general:
among these eleven characteristics, [the first] is the general one.
Each and every one takes intentionality as its very substance;
the fundamental consciousness serves as the supporting substance for all eleven consciousnesses, and it is exactly thus for each.
Second, regarding the specific [distinctions]:
Although there are eleven characteristics,
they are condensed into five;
these are the first four characteristics.
The common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) has the function of producing [the environment] without sensation;
its essence consists of the external retributive support (*niśraya-vipākaphala*), such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as their seeds.
The uncommon characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) has the function of producing [beings] with sensation; its essence consists of the seeds of the individual internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*).
The coarse and heavy characteristics and functions take all afflictions and the seeds of unwholesome states as their essence;
the subtle and light characteristics and functions take the outflowing [dharmas] such as faith as their essence;
and there are those that take the experience of karmic retribution as their essence.
The characteristic and function of the "unappropriated" (anupātta) have all afflictions as their essence.

The characteristic and function of the "metaphorical" (aupacārika) have the four inversions associated with the two consciousnesses of the intellect (manas) and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) as their essence.
Question:
With what intention is the characteristic of the representation of metaphorical designation established?
Answer:
The preceding non-apprehended characteristic arises from the perfuming of linguistic conventions (*nāma-vyavahāra*).
I have not yet clarified the beginning and end of the two consciousnesses—intentional and retributive—within the midst of delusion;
this is why I have come. [This concerns] whether they possess marks or lack marks.
The afflictions of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) constitute the characteristic of non-possession;
the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) constitute the substance of the characteristic of possession.
These two fetters are termed "substance": first, the fetter of heavy dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*).
The substance of delusion arises from the deluded mind;
it is termed "coarse," with the meaning being that of binding and fettering.
They are designated by way of their past experience.
Second, they are fetters (*saṃyojana*).
That which is called "clinging to signs" is termed a fetter because it binds one to signs.
They are named according to their objects and their faults. As for their substance, they take the afflictions of the mind and the afflictions of the "outer bark" as their substance.
Those of the mind have the mental factors as their nature;
those of the "outer bark" have the coarse and heavy [afflictions] as their substance.
The three afflictions, such as the skin and so forth, are designated by their substance. As for the designations:
first, the skin-affliction;
second, the flesh-affliction.
The three mental afflictions are both named after their metaphors and their faults. As for their substance,
if one discusses their substance according to the three aggregates:
Its substance consists solely of the habitual tendencies of the mind (*cittavāsanā*).
If its substance is derived from consciousness (*vijñāna*),
then the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) have all six consciousnesses as their substance.
The delusion of the mind has the mental consciousness alone as its substance.
If it is the delusion of the flesh, it takes as its substance the delusions arising from the apprehension by the mental consciousness of the two [other] consciousnesses.
These are the four kinds of worldly beings.
This refers to seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
Illuminating an object is called "seeing";
the subsequent arising of auditory consciousness is called "hearing."
The three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body are called "perception" (saṃjñā);
the mind is called "cognition" (vijñapti). As for its substance, it takes the six consciousnesses as its substance;
however, from the perspective of its fundamental basis, it takes only the mental consciousness as its substance.
Question:
Among the four [categories], which ones are the seven consciousnesses?
Answer:
Among the four [aspects], the first is called "knowledge.
The second aspect, which refers to the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), is called "essence" (*tattva*). The first is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
"dependent" refers to the capacity of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).
He is precisely that which can permeate (vāsanā).
All phenomena consist entirely of the object and the subject;
these two are the nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva).
The consciousness that cognizes objects is called "discrimination" (vikalpa);
this name is derived from its function.
Second is the nature of reality (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
It is called "true" because its essence is not like [that of other things];
it is called "real" because it lacks a substantial entity since it does not depend on others;
thus, these names are established through their distinct characteristics.
"Nature" (prakṛti) is so called because it is a fundamental category;
it is a name derived from its meaning. Second, regarding "substance" (tattva), I shall present it here according to one approach.
The dependent nature has the eighth consciousness as its essence;
the discriminating nature has the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, along with the habitual tendencies of the grasped objects, as its essence;
and the perfected nature has the four realities as its essence.
It has as its essence the suchness with stains and the stainless suchness, along with the stainless path and the twelvefold teaching.
Eleven are consciousnesses by name and essence. Regarding "name":
first, body-consciousness.
"Body" (kāya) has the meaning of being a basis;
it also has the meaning of an accumulation.
There are two kinds of bodies.
The seven consciousnesses are that which clings to the body.
Regarding the three feelings:
"feeling" (vedanā) refers to the function of receiving and taking in.
Fourth is "that which should be experienced" (*vedanīya*).
Objects are the spheres of consciousness;
thus, the meaning of "to be grasped" is termed "experienced."
The five types of correct reception (samāpatti) employ the meaning of "present manifestation" (pratibhāsa) in their current application;
they are all named according to their respective meanings.
Sixth, regarding "world" (*loka*):
phenomena possess movement, which is termed "world.
Furthermore, the distinctions between prior, middle, and posterior are termed "world."
It is named according to its temporal meaning;
it is the number seven.
That is to say, the dharmas possess the numerical designations of one, two, three, and so on.
The name is derived from its meaning.
Regarding the "eight bases" (*āyatana*):
the five great elements and other such factors are called "bases" (*sthāna*) because they are the locations upon which the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*) depends.
The name is derived from its meaning.
"Nine verbal expressions" refers to sounds that possess the capacity for designation (*abhilāpa*) regarding phenomena (*dharma*).
The detailed exposition is called the "Exposition of Names.
It is so named because it treats ten distinctions between self and others.
Self and other are defined by their mutual relation.
There are many different aspects to the distinction between self and other;
thus, "self" and "other" are names derived from this mutual relation and its meaning.
Eleventh, the two paths of good and evil:
that which accords with and benefits is called good;
that which opposes and harms is called evil.
The two are numerical categories (*saṃkhyā*), while the Path (*mārga*) is a name based on meaning (*artha*).
Thus, it receives its name from the meaning of its function and number. Regarding their essence (*svabhāva*), there is both a general and a specific sense.
If discussed in general terms,
these eleven consciousnesses take the mental objects of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as their nature.
If discussed specifically, however:
This is explained according to their respective characteristics.
Body-consciousness takes the five sense organs as its substance;
the body takes the seven consciousnesses as its substance.
Feeling has the mental realm (*manodhātu*) as its essence;
that which is to be felt has the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) as its essence;
and the actual experiencing has the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*) as its essence.
The world-number (loka-saṃkhyā) takes the eighteen elements (dhātus) as its substance;
the sense-bases (āyatanas) take the five great elements (mahābhūtas)— that is,
the four sensory objects— as their substance.
The distinction between self and other has as its essence the eighteen internal bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
The two paths of good and evil likewise have the eighteen bases and elements as their essence.
Regarding the meaning of the four consciousnesses, there is a twofold classification by way of two gates concerning name and essence. As for "name": [The text continues with the definition of names.]
It resembles the consciousness of objects (*viṣayavijñāna*).
Its luminous essence being non-existent is similar to the former mind, hence it is called "resembling" (*sadr̥śa*);
that which gives rise to consciousness is called the "object" (*viṣaya*).
It is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) because it arises through transformation;
this name is derived from both its object and its essence.
The second is the consciousness resembling the sense organs (indriya).
The "resembling consciousness" is the same as before.
"Dominant" (adhipati) is the meaning of "faculty" (indriya);
it is named according to its functional significance.
Third, it resembles the consciousness of a self.
"Self" refers to the conceptualization that a person has a substantial entity, which is designated as the "self";
the [consciousness] receives its name from the meaning of that entity.
Fourth, it is "resembling consciousness" (vijñapti-sadṛśa).
Consciousness is the function of discernment;
it is named after this function. Second is its essence (svabhāva).
It takes the consciousnesses of the six objects, such as form and so forth, as its substance.
Regarding the object of dharmas (*dharmāyatana*), it generally encompasses the transformations of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
If one distinguishes the substance based on the eleven consciousnesses, [the analysis is as follows].
Regarding the statement that the locus of worldly enumeration should be understood as having consciousness as its essence:
the consciousness resembling the sense organs has the six roots as its essence;
among the eleven types of consciousness, that which takes up the body has the experiencer as its essence.
The function of the semblance of self-consciousness (*ātman-vijñapti*) takes the grasping of two dharmas as its essence;
among the eleven consciousnesses, it takes the differentiation between self and other as its essence.
The function of the semblance of object-consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñapti*) takes the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as its essence.
Among the eleven consciousnesses, the consciousness that takes up meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and the body take as their essence the aspect of apprehending and discerning objects.
This applies to all four consciousnesses throughout both the wholesome and unwholesome paths.
At this time, they are analyzed according to three meanings and two gates.
First, the name;
second, the essence. Regarding the name:
first, the time of equality.
When the mind is clarified, it departs from high and low and proceeds toward correct equality;
"departing from faults" is its name.
This occurs at the time when the two are in union.
The convergence of the two minds—the speaker’s and the listener’s—is called "harmony" (*saṃnipāta*);
it is named according to its meaning.
This occurs during the three revolutions of the wheel.
It clarifies that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, which enables sentient beings to receive the Eightfold Noble Path, is similar to the wheel of worldly existence.
It is named after its metaphorical basis. Second, regarding its essence:
it takes the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and the great compassionate mind (*mahākaruṇā-citta*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as its essence.
The externalists establish three meanings for the existence of form (*rūpa*): first, that form already exists prior to the arising of visual consciousness;
second, that what is transformed by consciousness into form is also form;
and third, that because the mind cognizes form, one knows that form exists.
The four modes of birth are distinguished by way of two gates: name and essence. Regarding the names:
first is birth from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*).
"Womb" (*jarāyu*) refers to the beginning.
They may be named according to their time,
or they may also be named according to their characteristics.
Second, moisture-born beings.
The soaking and saturation by water is called moisture (*sneha*).
It arises from that [water] and is named after its basis.
First, birth from an egg.
This refers to the single egg within the shell;
it is named according to its characteristic feature.
Fourth, apparitional birth (*upapāduka*).
Because the sense faculties (*indriya*) arise instantaneously, it is called "apparitional" (*nirmāṇa*);
because birth occurs through such apparition, it is called "apparitional birth."
The name is derived from its meaning;
it is generally termed "birth" (*jāti*).
The name is established based on the sense of "kind" or "category."
They may also be designated by way of their fruit. Regarding their essential nature:
those born from a womb take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the desire realm as their nature;
those born from moisture, the transformational, and the egg-born are likewise.
The nature of the five aggregates born by transformation within the three realms.
Question:
What is formless and what is not formless?
How is it that those born by transformation possess the five aggregates?
Answer:
According to the Hīnayāna school.
There are no formless realms (*ārūpya*) that are not subsumed within the four modes of birth (*yoni*).
Now, according to the Mahāyāna,
because there is also form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms, they possess all five aggregates (*skandha*).
According to the *Yingluo jing* (Sūtra of the Necklace), there is transformation-birth (*upapāduka*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Therefore, this transformation-birth extends throughout the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
Regarding the meaning, name, and essence of the four elements (*catvāri dhātavaḥ*): as for the "name":
The names and essences of the three realms have already been presented as before.
As for the fourth, the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*): "taint" (*āsrava*) refers to that which flows [into cyclic existence].
It is called a "realm" (dhātu) because it arises from that which is free from outflows;
it is named after its faultlessness and its meaning.
Its essence consists of the transformed five aggregates (pañca-skandha) of a bodhisattva.
The six elements are distinguished by way of two gates: name and substance.
As for the names, they are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness;
these are the six great elements.
The term "dhātu" (element) signifies both "nature" and "cause.
It is designated by way of its functional meaning. Regarding the two entities:
the former four are subsumed within the sense-object of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*).
It takes the consciousness of form as its essence.
The great element of space takes the vast void and the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) as its essence;
yet, insofar as it is a transformation of the mind, it is considered conditioned (*samskrta*) from the perspective of the mind.
In the Hīnayāna, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are invariably empty.
As for the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*), if it is taken in its primary sense, it consists solely of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
if it is taken in a broader sense that includes the auxiliary factors of illumination, it encompasses all seven consciousnesses.
If one discusses it in terms of its basis and support, it pervades the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);
however, it takes only that which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and with outflows (*sāsrava*), and does not take that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
This is because it arises within the three realms; such is its very nature.
Regarding the names and entities of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*):
as for the "names," the six consciousnesses— namely, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—
are all named after their respective sense organs.
The six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) encompass all phenomena;
they are namely form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects (*dharmas*).
The six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are namely eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. As for these two entities:
The six objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) have as their nature both form-consciousness (rūpavijñāna) and consciousness itself (vijñāna).
As for the mind-faculty (manas), that which arises subsequent to the six consciousnesses is all termed "mind";
thus, it encompasses all six consciousnesses.
If we clarify the meaning according to the mental door (*manodvāra*),
the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the seven consciousnesses all possess the sense of "arising" and are thus all termed "roots" (*indriya*).
The first five [consciousnesses] have only form as their essence, while the [sixth] consciousness has cognition as its essence.
If one takes the fundamental nature of the six consciousnesses, they have the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as their essence.
Because it is established that there is only a single mental consciousness, the existence of five distinct essences for the [sensory] consciousnesses is not admitted.
While there are six [consciousnesses] according to their functions, this [single essence] has no such correspondence.
The essence of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) consists of the six faculties and the six objects.
Since the six consciousnesses are included within the mental faculty (*manas*),
these constitute the twelve bases.
Consciousness arises through the gateway of understanding;
since both faculties and objects arise, its substance is identical to the eighteen realms.
The five aggregates are likewise so.
The five faculties and the five objects enter into the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
The six consciousnesses and the mental faculty (manas) enter into the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
The mental object (dharmadhātu) enters into three aggregates as its constituent parts.
These three categories of dharmas:
their intrinsic nature is the *dhātu*;
they give rise to consciousness; and they are the spheres of entry (*āyatana*).
The meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is "accumulation.
The meaning of the three types of observation of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) is termed its "substance. Regarding "name":
first, it is "mere-measure" (*pramāṇa-mātra*).
The second consists of only two;
the third consists of three types.
Regarding the term "only quantity" (pramāṇa-mātra):
The term "only" (vijñapti-mātra) refers to the measure of consciousness;
it is named after its object.
As for the expression "only two":
Second is enumeration (*saṃkhyā*);
it is named according to its meaning and its number.
Third is variety (*nānātva*); that is, the objects and phenomena are not of one kind, hence they are called "various."
"Kind" (lei) refers to a category;
it is named according to its meaning.
"Contemplation" (guan) is named according to the meaning of observation.

Furthermore, the three contemplations may both be named according to their objects and the mind, because the contemplation is the mind itself, while [the realization that it is] "merely representation" (*vijñaptimātra*) and so forth constitutes the object. Second, regarding their essence:
although the three contemplations are the same in taking hearing, reflection, and cultivation as their essence.

If, during the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and within the stages themselves, it takes the three types of wisdom—namely, that derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and so forth—as its essence;
then, upon actually entering the stages, it takes the wisdom of realization through correct cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) as its essence.
The two meanings of "bodilessness" refer to its essence and substance: first, the absence of a material body;
second, the absence of a birth-body.
"Materiality" (rūpa) takes obstruction as its defining characteristic.
Birth is called "birth" because it arises together with the mind;
it does not have a name that exists independently of meaning.
Names arise from both meaning and characteristics.
The general name "body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of "basis.
It is designated according to its functional capacity. Regarding the two types of bodies:
the formless body takes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as its causal basis and essence.
The statement "non-existent" refers to grasping at a non-substantial body;
its essence consists of the four aggregates (*skandhas*) which lack the causes and conditions for arising.
The statement "non-body" likewise refers to grasping at the non-substantial four aggregates.
Regarding the meaning, names, and essence of the four wisdoms of Vijñaptimātra:
as for the names,
the first is the knowledge of the differing characteristics of consciousness.
The knower is the bodhisattva’s contemplation of the mind;
the characteristic of contradictory cognitions is the object.
Second, it is because one perceives that consciousness has no objective realm.
The word "by" (yōu) means that what is already known is the wisdom that knows;
consciousness without an object is that which is observed.
Third, it is by knowing the absence of effortful application.
Through the understanding derived from the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), one knows that this is simply the mundane state.
Because it is free from effort (*anābhoga*) and should result in the attainment of correct gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*), it is called "free from effort.
This name is derived from both the capacity for cognition and its object.
Fourth, by knowing that the meaning follows along with the three types of wisdom.
This [term] and the previous two are both named according to their mental objects and states;
they may also be named according to their mental objects, states, and meanings. Second, as for their essential natures:
These four have the nature of mental understanding through the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and not anything else;
they may also generally take the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) as their essence.
Regarding the names and essences of the sixteen truths: as for "name" (*nāman*):
Below "suffering" (duḥkha) there are four aspects:
namely, suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self.
"Suffering" has the meaning of being oppressed.
Constant flux and instability is impermanence.
Emptiness is the absence of anything existing, which is why it is called "empty.
Lack of sovereignty is non-self.
"Emptiness" (śūnyatā) is named after its absence of another;
the remaining three are named after what has passed.
Below "origination" (samudaya), there are four.
"Dependent origination through causes and conditions" means that "cause" (hetu) signifies the sense of a means for arising,
while "origination" (samudaya) signifies the sense of collective arising.
That which "possesses" (sat) is so named because it possesses the capacity for its future fruit;
that which is a "condition" (pratyaya) is so named because it can act as a condition for the fruit.
Both derive their names from their functional efficacy.
Below "Way" (Dao) there are four [entries]:
namely, Way, Suchness, Trace, and Vehicle.
"Way" takes the meaning of facilitating the passage of sentient beings.
The traces of conduct practiced by the sages are conveyed by means of the vehicle of liberation;
it is no different from the meaning [of reality].
The Buddhas of the three periods of time do not differ from this path; therefore, it is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
This name is derived from its essential meaning.
The other three names are derived from their functional capacities.
Cessation is fourfold:
namely, cessation, tranquility, excellence, and detachment.
The cessation of the three poisons is called "cessation."
"Correct" (*zheng*) refers to the cessation of the three fires.
"Subtle extinction" (*miaomie*) is the essence of non-existence;
the name "subtle" (*miao*) is derived from its meaning.
"Detachment" has the meaning of being free from delusion.
These three are designated by names that are beyond fault.
"Truth" (satya) has the meaning of reality.
The name is derived from its meaning. Regarding the two natures, there are two [ways of] establishing them:
first, establishing the nature in terms of the actual phenomena (*vastu*).
This means that suffering and so forth constitute the very nature of suffering and so forth.
This refers to the meaning of "fruit.
Its essence consists of the four factors of karma, afflictions, and so forth.
Its functional aspect consists of the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*).
It pervades both matter and mind;
its essence is cessation through deliberation, which is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Second, regarding that which is pervasive and transcendent:
That is to say, the essence consists of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the originally enlightened mind.
The five kinds of reality refer to the essence of practice, which are taught as the five realities by way of being free from the five kinds of discursive movement.
Furthermore, because they are free from the discrimination of the five consciousnesses, they are also called the five kinds of non-differentiation.
It takes non-conceptual concentration and wisdom as its essence;
the fivefold classification is taught in terms of the abandonment of hindrances.
In the *Buddhatva-śāstra*, these five types do not differ significantly from one another.
First, it is unconditioned;
second, it is without differentiation;
third, it is free from the two extremes.
The four liberations,
the fivefold natural purity,
and the five kinds of reality.
First, non-duality;
second, the transcendence of verbal expression;
third, the transcendence of vitarka and vicāra.
Fourth, the refutation of identity and difference.
Fifth, the single flavor of purity.
Third, the differentiation of names and entities: names.
First is the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*),
which refers to the five consciousnesses;
"self" is a term that distinguishes itself from others.
Nature (*svabhāva*) may also be understood as the essence (*tattva*);
thus, "nature" is a designation based on the meaning of "essence.
Second, mindfulness and retention (*dhāraṇā*).
To pursue an object is called "recollection" (smṛti).
To maintain it without forgetting is called "retention" (dhāraṇā).
These are named according to their functions.
Third, there is "manifestation.
Manifestation means that an object does not exist at present, yet manifestation causes it to be named as existing;
this is a name derived from its function. As for "essence," there are two different meanings.
The first is the Hīnayāna.
Its intrinsic nature has the mental factors of awakening as its essence;
its essence consists of mindfulness following recollection.
This demonstrates that its nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the two bodies of the Mahāyāna:
the self-nature consists of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
All [of these] have present objects and are exclusively *svabhāva-vikalpa* (intrinsic conceptualization).
The remaining two types belong solely to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Taking the past as their object constitutes "retention" (*dhāraṇa*).
The discrimination that takes the future as its object is presented to demonstrate discrimination itself.
It is said to be twofold:
first, the various perfuming latencies are each distinct.
"Self" (sva) means that each arises from its own cause;
secondly, because all phenomena (*dharma*) do not exist in reality and arise from the mind, they are merely called "self.

As for their essence (*tattva*), it takes the pure and impure categories of phenomena as its substance. How is this distinguished? It is simply like the characteristics of the myriad things, rather than the characteristic of a single thing.

Question: What is the intention? Since the fundamental consciousness-mind originally has no mind, why does it not remain as a single signless state, but instead manifest as the signs of these myriad phenomena?
[The six causes] are named and defined as follows: Name.
First, the objective field (*ālambana*).
A phenomenon that can give rise to the mind is called an objective field;
this is the meaning of "arising."
