The name is derived from its meaning.
Second, regarding "characteristics" (*nimitta*):
this clarifies that the mind apprehends the specific features of objects.
The name is derived from its meaning:
"contemplative vision.
It refers to the clear discernment and swift judgment of the mind; thus, it is termed "contemplative vision."
The name is derived from its meaning.
There are four types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); that which is the condition for the arising of retribution is called dependent origination.
It is designated as "speech" by way of conventional designation.
The sound that proclaims it is called "name," and because speech brings about comprehension, it is called "expression."
These are also designated by way of skillful means.
Sixth is "superimposition" (*samāropa*):
to cling to the principle of the three natures as having a self or phenomena is called superimposition.
Regarding the name derived from its past [function] and its essence (*tattva*):
if the essence is clarified in terms of consciousness, it takes the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as its essence;
if the essence is derived from the three delusions, it has the delusion of mind-only (*cittamātra*) as its nature.
The meaning of the three types of perfuming consists of their names and essences: first, the perfuming of names (*nāma-vāsanā*).
Sound that possesses expressive denotation is called "speech" (*vyavahāra*); it is named according to its meaning.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is so named because its perfuming consists of the act of discerning (*vijñapti*).
It is named according to its function.
Second is the consciousness of form (*rūpa-vijñāna*).
"Form" (*rūpa*) has the meaning of resistance (*pratigha*).
Taking its essential nature as its name,
it is "consciousness" (vijñāna);
it cognizes, and the six consciousnesses are its functional applications.
The subsequent consciousness is its very substance;
it is named according to its substance and function.
As for the "seeing-consciousness" (darśana-vijñāna), it refers to the perfuming of habit-energies (vāsanā).
The clarity of its own name is "view" (dṛṣṭi);
the essence of view is named "consciousness" (vijñāna), and the designation is the same as before.
Third, the afflictions (kleśa).
It is named after what has passed.
As for "action" (karman),
it is called action because of its nature of performing or constructing.
It is named according to its function.
As for "fruition" (vipāka),
it is called "fruit" because it recompenses the cause.
Thus, it is named according to its function;
the name is derived from its meaning. Regarding the two natures:
the first five [afflictions] have the deluded mind as their essential nature.
The afflictions take the two delusions of skin and flesh as their essence;
karma takes the three types of action as its nature,
or alternatively, it may take the three aggregates as its nature.
The fruit-retribution [aspect] takes the five aggregates as its substance.
Regarding the term "substance" (tattva) used here in the sense of "category" (jāti) and "meaning" (artha) in relation to the dependent nature: there are two kinds of category and meaning.
First, the category of fruit-retribution.
That which recompenses causes is called "fruit" (*phala*); that which follows from causes is called "retribution" (*vipāka*);
and that which serves as a support for others is called "substance" (*svabhāva*).
"Category" (jāti) refers to a class or type;
it is so designated because, in relation to other phenomena, it is not singular,
and it receives its name from the sense of its basis, its capacity, and its functional utility.
Second, regarding the nature and categories of hearing, reflection, and so forth:
their names are identical, but they are distinguished as mundane and supramundane. Second, regarding their essence:

Although it is divided into two based on the dependent [subject], its substance is, in all cases, the fundamental consciousness—the single mind—as its essential nature. Second, regarding the meaning of "dependent" (paratantra):
this clarifies that although this consciousness is divided into two based on its substance, [it remains dependent].
However, these two factors do not each exclusively serve as the object-condition for a single mind.
Because they do not each exclusively serve as the object of a single mind, they are termed "dependent" (*paratantra*).
[Next,] the names and essences of the two meanings and two gates of conceptualization (*parikalpita*) are as follows.
First is the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
It consists of knowing that the essence of other phenomena is distinct and not shared with others,
and it functions to distinguish them from others through the mind.
The essence of nature is its substance;
consciousness, when taking this object as its condition, is called "discrimination.
This is a designation based on the characteristics, substance, and function [of that object].
It may also be used exclusively as a name;
secondly, the consciousness that discerns distinctions possesses clear understanding.
